articles.title_orig: No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls show
articles.title_zh: No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls show
articles.content_orig:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu casts his ballot, alongside his wife Sara, at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot , appear short of an outright victory, initial exit polls indicate.
Israelis flocked to polling stations Tuesday to decide the political fate of Netanyahu , the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister who is facing one of the most consequential tests of his political career.
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis were able to cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Numbers from Israel's Central Elections ​Committee reflected a strong turnout, with 66.7% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 6 p.m., local time—the highest turnout logged at that time since 1973.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his own ballot just after midday, at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
Not long after, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he again urged people to go out and vote.
Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had submitted a request to the Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past 10 p.m. The committee later announced it would not be extending voting hours past the scheduled closing time.
This is the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip . Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran , backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen .
The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty.
Read More: Israel's Choice
“I hope this will be a true holiday for democracy,” Isaac Herzog, the Israeli head of state, told reporters from a polling station in Rehavia, where he and his wife voted. “No one can be allowed to spoil or undermine it.”
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
The Democrats party on Tuesday said Golan had been “approached in a threatening manner” by a man who was found to be carrying a knife. The lawmaker was attending a voting-day mobilization tour in Tel Aviv's HaMesila Park at the time of the incident.
"Golan’s security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground," the party said in a statement shared with the Guardian . "Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect." Golan, in his own statement, vowed that "incitement and violence will not deter us" and encouraged people to go out and vote.
Meanwhile, some polls had suggested that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also projected that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition were likely to win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates . Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout. However, on Tuesday, there appeared to be strong turnout in some of Israel’s largest Arab-majority towns.
A cyclist rides beneath a pedestrian bridge displaying electronic election billboards showing former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot (L) and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 23, 2026. Erik Marmor—picture alliance/Getty Images
Netanyahu has brought attention to the support he received from his longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump , who only announced his endorsement days before the election as conflict in the Middle East has tested their friendship.
In a late-night TV appearance on Oct. 25 , Netanyahu boasted of Trump’s endorsement and said that Trump was willing to take action “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat” so long as Netanyahu stayed in power. Netanyahu added that he has already instructed Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad as well as the IDF to “bring down” the Iranian regime. Trump remains very popular in Israel.
By contrast, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu for re-election, just a day after Trump put his “complete and total” support behind the Israeli leader.
“The President has the most effective endorsement in American, or international, political history,” said Vance, when asked in an interview if he would also be extending an endorsement of his own. “I endorse American candidates and that’s where I'm focused on, is the midterms, so I'm not getting involved in the Israeli elections.”
When pushed for an answer, Vance added: “I'm not anti-endorsing [Netanyahu], I'm not pro-endorsing him.”
At stake for Netanyahu could be more than his continued leadership. The premier faces an international arrest warrant for alleged crimes related to the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. And even domestically, critics have demanded an inquiry into Netanyahu’s decision-making around Oct. 7. The attack, which resulted in over 1,200 people in Israel killed and around 250 hostages taken, is considered by many to be indicative of a major security failure.
The Gaza health ministry reports that since Oct. 7, 2023, more than 74,000 individuals have been killed. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, Gaza’s health ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME.
Another issue driving the election is public fury over ultra-Orthodox communities’ exemption from military conscription for men engaged in religious studies. articles.title_orig: Alibaba wins preliminary injunction against Pentagon lobbying rule
articles.title_zh: Alibaba wins preliminary injunction against Pentagon lobbying rule
articles.content_orig:
Judge finds company likely to succeed on free-speech challenge, but leaves tech giant’s Chinese military designation intact
Alibaba has won a preliminary court order blocking a US restriction that drove away its Washington lobbyists, after a federal judge found the Chinese technology giant was likely to succeed in challenging the measure on free-speech grounds.
US District Judge Eumi K. Lee ruled on Monday that the government had failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify the restriction, which effectively forces lobbying firms to choose between representing Alibaba and clients seeking Pentagon contracts.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

Programme designed to prop up the Northern Mariana Islands’ economy axed as Republicans campaign on immigration enforcement
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Monday the suspension of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorisation Programme.
US Senator Mike Lee hailed the move on social media, calling the programme a “Biden-era loophole for Chinese birth tourism” and praising the Trump administration for having “closed” the pathway.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends higher on revived AI momentum
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends higher on revived AI momentum
articles.content_orig:
The tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.
Anthropic's IPO filing on Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies.
It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said a debut likely won't take place until 2027.
Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs of jitters on the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and for SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same.
Now, all eyes turn to Anthropic , which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services.
"If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.
Anthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions at Microsoft , Amazon and Alphabet , which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued to Amazon , Broadcom and Google , while Microsoft and Nvidia agreed to invest $15 billion as the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices , Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development.
Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed to backstopping Anthropic for a data center in Texas. Broadcom , which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.
For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants like Adobe and Salesforce that have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.
And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever.
"If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."
Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco and Elon Musk's SpaceX , which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth.
Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier.
The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter.
"It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."
One source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.
In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.
Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis.
"I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other."
With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.
"Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.
A lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.
David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available."
"If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote.
Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an industry benchmark .
Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential.
"Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."
Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu.
"We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.

articles.title_orig: Robinhood shares fall 5% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
articles.title_zh: Robinhood shares fall 5% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
articles.content_orig:
Robinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.
Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.
Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.
Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.
Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.
Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.
Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.
—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

articles.title_orig: UPS Stock Jumps After Earnings Deliver Good News for the U.S. Economy
articles.title_zh: UPS Stock Jumps After Earnings Deliver Good News for the U.S. Economy
articles.content_orig:
One word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient."
That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success.
The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $6.52 per gallon in September, would drive up prices on consumer products . Economists also worried that more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending.
Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales.
"There's been a lot of noise in the market this year. There's a lot of geopolitical stuff," Royal Caribbean Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday. "But I look at our business [and our results], and I think that really talks to the resilience of the business, the resilience of the consumer."
Royal Caribbean reported an increase in bookings during its third quarter, while Sherwin-Williams' CEO said the quarter was evidence of the company's strength.
Here's how companies are reading the consumer in the most recent three-month period:
The food and beverage company beat analysts' expectations for third-quarter earnings and revenue despite what CEO Henrique Braun called an "uneven environment."
Coca-Cola reported that North America unit case volume was flat, indicating demand was steady in the face of higher prices. The company's overall unit case volume was helped by higher demand outside of North America.
"The underlying momentum remains quite strong," Chief Financial Officer John Murphy told CNBC. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."
The company increased its full-year forecast and now expects its comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from a prior forecast of growth between 9% and 10%.
The cruise company beat Wall Street's expectations for earnings per share and narrowly missed on revenue.
"Our third quarter results reflect continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences and the accelerated momentum across our industry leading brands," CEO Liberty said in the release .
The company reported that the number of guests served in the third quarter increased 9% year over year to 2.7 million vacationers and said booking volumes for 2027 were already "up in the high teens," pacing ahead of historical levels and indicating high travel demand.
"It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back as relates to the vacation experiences," Liberty told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" following the report.
Royal Caribbean shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.
Sherwin-Williams beat analysts' expectations for revenue but fell short of expected earnings per share.
Sherwin-Williams CEO Heidi Petz said in the company's earnings release that the paint retailer's performance demonstrated "the resilience of our Company and the strength of our strategy in a challenging demand environment."
"Despite muted underlying market volumes, we continued to win new customers, increase share-of-wallet and deliver sales growth across all three reportable segments," she said.
Net sales increased 7.9% from the same period last year. The company attributed the gain to higher selling prices, but the benefits to profits were partially offset by increased costs of raw materials and supply-chain related expenses.
And the company maintained full-year guidance, saying "customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027."
UPS beat Wall Street expectations for both earnings per share and revenue in the third quarter.
Revenue in the U.S. rose 4.5% during the period to $14.86 billion.
CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the company's earnings call that consumers remain "resilient" ahead of the holiday season, the company's busiest period. She said the company expects that average daily shipping volume will grow next quarter at a rate consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume will likely fall due to reducing deliveries with Amazon, she said.
UPS has been in the midst of unwinding its partnership with Amazon at the same time it's executing a broad turnaround effort to operate more leanly.
The company raised its full-year forecast for the second quarter in a row, projecting consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion.
Shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.
Not every company is seeing the same spending trends, however.
Appliance maker Whirlpool missed on both the top and bottom lines for its third quarter and cut its full-year revenue guidance.
Net sales in North America fell more than 8% year over year during the period ending on Sept. 30.
Even still, the company cited its own read on "resilience."
"Through disciplined working capital management, we are protecting our year end free cash flow and our balance sheet resilience to navigate challenging market conditions," CFO Roxanne Warner said in the earnings release .
Shares closed up more than 3% on Tuesday.
— CNBC's Amelia Lucas and Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.title_zh: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.content_orig:
The State Department has ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to evacuate Saudi Arabia following a surge in missile and drone strikes targeting civilian airports and critical infrastructure across the kingdom.
In a security alert issued Tuesday, the U.S. warned that ongoing hostilities by Iran-backed Houthi forces have caused severe travel disruptions and civilian casualties, prompting strict travel restrictions for American personnel and warnings of wider regional spillover.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," according to the alert.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
Flight operations remain severely disrupted across major transit hubs, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport , where only limited routes are running, alongside significant delays at facilities in Jeddah and Dammam.
U.S. officials urged private citizens to exercise extreme caution, consider overland transit alternatives via operational borders like the King Fahd Causeway, and strictly abide by local regulations barring the filming or sharing of attack sites and counter-missile activity.
Israelis turned out in exceptionally high numbers Tuesday for the country’s first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, with initial exit polls showing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud emerging as the largest party but his governing coalition falling short of a parliamentary majority, potentially opening the door to a change in leadership.
The projections released by Israel’s three major television networks after polls closed at 10 p.m. local time (4 p.m. ET) showed Likud winning 25 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 23 seats for former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party in Channels 12 and 13 exit polls, and 21 seats according to Kan 11.
The projected parliamentary balance showed 50 seats for Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc, 53 for the main opposition parties and 17 for Arab parties, leaving neither major bloc with the 61 seats generally needed to form a government.
Although Netanyahu’s party is projected to remain the largest in parliament, his political future is far from secure.
The opposition parties, together with the Arab factions, would hold a combined 70 seats, although that does not mean they would necessarily agree to form a government together.
This is an excerpt from a report by Fox News Digital's Efrat Lachter.
President Donald Trump declared Tuesday that attacking Iran was one of the greatest things he had ever done while defending his decision to go to war with the country he described as "lunatic."
"We had to stop this lunatic nation from having a nuclear weapon," Trump said during a rally at the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas.
"It's not like, oh, gee, let's not do it. If we did that, we might not be here right now, to be honest.
"But at some point in the not too distant future, really bad things would have happened," Trump added.
"Somebody asked me yesterday, it's very interesting, ‘If you had to do it again would you have attacked Iran?’
"I said, ‘one of the greatest things I ever did.’ Short term, short term pain," he added.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the war with Iran would end soon before claiming U.S. forces had destroyed hundreds of Iranian military aircraft and naval vessels.
“It's going to end very soon,” Trump said Tuesday during a rally at the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas.
“They have no military. They have no air force.
“Their navy, 159 ships on the bottom of the sea.
“‘Sir, we've knocked out 159 ships.’ I said, ‘How many do they have?’ 159, sir.
“We've knocked out 288 jet fighters. How many do they have? So they have 288," he said.
“You know where their fighters are?” Trump asked. “They're scattered all over the runways,” he said.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the United States is on the verge of victory over Iran, accusing past American leaders of lacking the courage or intelligence to confront Tehran over its nuclear ambitions.
“We're now in the throes of having an even greater victory against Iran and stopping them from ever having a nuclear weapon,” Trump said during remarks at the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas.
“And you've got to understand that America did not start the war with Iran. Iran has been waging this war against America since 1979, killing many, many of our great people," he added.
“They've killed thousands of our soldiers and wounded so many more,” Trump said, referring to injuries involving “the legs, the limbs, the face.”
“And those people are many of them are living now, but they're living a hard life."
“Past leaders should have settled this problem long ago, but they didn't have the courage or intelligence to do it," the president said.
The United Kingdom updated its travel advisory for Iran on Tuesday, warning of a high risk of sudden escalation in the Middle East and expanding its guidance to British nationals traveling in the region.
The British Foreign Office described the situation as “deeply unpredictable,” strengthening its previous description of “unpredictable.”
"Since conflict began in early 2026, Iran has stated its intention to target locations associated with the US and Israel, including, but not limited to, organisations, businesses, facilities, and institutions," the advisory states.
The updated guidance also refers to strikes and retaliatory attacks by “Iran and others,” rather than Iran alone.
The Foreign Office also reiterated its warning against all travel to Iran, urging British nationals already in the country to consider the risks of remaining.
"British and British-Iranian dual nationals are at significant risk of arrest, questioning or detention," the advisory warns, adding that having a British passport or ties to the U.K. can be grounds for detention.
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi warned the U.N. Security Council on Tuesday that the agency cannot verify whether Iran has diverted nuclear material before urging Tehran to grant inspectors access to key nuclear facilities and stockpiles.
"One area of particular concern is Iran’s previously declared nuclear material — which includes 440 kg of high-enriched uranium,” Grossi said in a statement .
“The Agency has been unwavering in its efforts to engage with Iran so that Iran provides the necessary information and grants IAEA inspectors access to facilities to verify the status of this material, as is required under the NPT Safeguards Agreement."
"As of today, the IAEA has not been able to verify that there has been no diversion of nuclear material required to be safeguarded under Iran’s CSA," Grossi said in a statement.
Grossi said Iran has repeatedly refused IAEA requests to access the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, which Tehran declared shortly before military strikes began in June 2025.
Grossi urged Iran to provide the information and access needed to verify its nuclear material and facilities, calling compliance with its safeguards obligations a legal requirement.
President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday praised the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as a founding pillar of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), telling delegates in Moscow that Russia remembers Iran’s former supreme leader "with gratitude."
"You have quite rightly mentioned the role of the late Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was indeed one of the most active participants in the establishment of our forum, and we rightly remember this with gratitude," Putin said, according to Iranian state-run Press TV .
Iran was central to the forum’s origins, with the initiative first proposed in Tehran in 2001 and the organization formally established in 2008.

On Monday, Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE: VZ ) CEO Dan Schulman sees opportunities to collaborate with satellite providers such as Elon Musk's Starlink , but says the wireless carrier has no reason to let Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ) use its network to compete for mobile customers .
Speaking during Verizon's third-quarter earnings call, Schulman acknowledged that satellite connectivity could complement traditional wireless services, particularly in remote areas with limited cellular coverage.
"I do think there is a role for satellite for sure in remote areas. It's a great service for those customers," he said, adding, "And I do think there are ways that we can work together, either directly or through our JV with satellite providers, to provide a complementary service and a differentiated value proposition."
Schulman reiterated that the company has no plans to offer satellite providers access to its network through mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) agreements.
"I will say, and I'll repeat it again, that there are no backdoors to any of our MVNO agreements and I see absolutely no benefit whatsoever to extending an MVNO deal to any satellite provider," he added.
An MVNO, or mobile virtual network operator, sells wireless services using another carrier's network rather than relying entirely on its own infrastructure.

During the call, Schulman said Verizon takes SpaceX's ambitions seriously and assumes the company will execute its plans successfully.
He argued that competing directly with established wireless carriers would require SpaceX to build a substantial terrestrial network, including 65,000 to 80,000 macro sites, backhaul infrastructure, radio access equipment and significant spectrum resources.
Schulman estimated that such a buildout could take at least four to six years and cost $300 billion to $500 billion over seven to eight years.
He also dismissed the idea that Verizon must offer Starlink network access to prevent rivals from gaining an advantage.
"There is no benefit to Verizon Communications extending an MVNO deal," Schulman said, adding that the company intends to compete aggressively if SpaceX enters the market. "We will punch back hard when that happens," he said.

articles.title_orig: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Isn’t Fast Enough.
articles.title_zh: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Isn’t Fast Enough.
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected because of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock fell 10% in trading Tuesday.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster, but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 20 states filed a lawsuit on Monday against Dollar General over alleged deceptive pricing practices.
The FTC and states claimed that Dollar General, over a period of years, had repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers and failed to correct the issue despite corporate knowledge of the problem. Dollar General has disputed those claims.
Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement that "Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last."
"The FTC's action underscores the agency's commitment to lowering costs for consumers by stopping deceptive pricing practices that harm Americans," Mufarrige added.
INSTACART AGREES TO $60M CONSUMER REFUNDS AFTER FTC ACCUSES COMPANY OF HIDDEN FEES AND FORCED SUBSCRIPTIONS
Dollar General was hit with a lawsuit by the FTC and 20 states over alleged deceptive pricing practices. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The complaint said that thousands of Dollar General stores have taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice.
It added that the company has received tens of thousands of complaints from consumers across the country who said the company didn't honor the advertised price , which suggests there has been widespread consumer harm to shoppers around the country.
States that joined the FTC lawsuit include Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
FTC DECLARES JULY AS 'MADE IN THE USA' MONTH
Dollar General disputed the claims made in the FTC complaint and said the proposed settlement was excessive. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Dollar General disputed the claims made in the suit filed by the FTC and states, saying in a statement that "The lawsuit filed today by the Federal Trade Commission and several states suggests that we have abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers. Nothing could be further from the truth."
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store. As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer," Dollar General said.
The company's statement said that it was made aware of the FTC investigation in early February 2026 and that it "engaged cooperatively" with the FTC and made several company representatives available to provide sworn testimony on relatively short notice.
WANT TO CANCEL A SUBSCRIPTION? FTC FINALIZES RULE TO MAKE IT EASIER FOR CONSUMERS
Dollar General said that after the FTC concluded sworn testimony, it received a draft complaint along with a draft settlement which demanded a monetary amount that was "untethered to – and orders of magnitude larger than – any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said that it worked in good faith with the FTC over the next four weeks and explained its issues with the agency's findings, then made a counteroffer for a monetary settlement before the agency filed suit.

articles.title_orig: Report: iPhone 18 Pro sales down 4% in the US, but China drives 3.1% global growth
articles.title_zh: Report: iPhone 18 Pro sales down 4% in the US, but China drives 3.1% global growth
articles.content_orig:
Counterpoint Research’s latest report offers a look at global iPhone 18 Pro sales during the first three weeks of availability. Here are the details.
In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max sales in the US fell 4% during their first three weeks of availability compared to the first three weeks of iPhone 17 Pro series sales last year.
The report noted that Japan saw a whopping 27% drop in sales, with demand weakening “as exchange rates amplified the price increases.”
China, on the other hand, saw a 29% increase in sales, while other markets collectively recorded a more modest 3.1% increase.
The report doesn’t break down what that means in units, or millions of units, but it does offer some context on what drove these regional differences.
A regional breakdown shows that the global 3.1% growth was concentrated in specific markets. China posted the strongest growth, with sales rising 29% YoY. This was driven by better early supply compared with last year and by price increases on competing flagship models from Chinese Android OEMs. Excluding China’s contribution, the global sales growth rate would have been far weaker. The US and Japan experienced a YoY decline, affected by higher prices compared with their predecessors. In the US, consumers largely do not perceive meaningful improvements over the previous models in either features or design, while in Japan, demand has contracted as exchange rates amplified the price increases.
Today’s report also includes another interesting tidbit: According to Counterpoint, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for a slightly smaller share of Pro-series sales compared to last year’s iPhone 17 Pro series, which the firm attributed to higher prices and stronger demand for the smaller Pro model in emerging markets:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for 56% of sales within the iPhone 18 Pro series, a slight decrease from 57% last year. This can be attributed to the higher prices compared with last year, as well as the fact that the sales growth in emerging markets such as India and Southeast Asia skewed more toward the Pro models.
As to how, or whether, the iPhone Duo had any effect on these shifting numbers, the report didn’t address that directly, since the device launched after the three-week period covered by the data. However, Counterpoint Associate Director Sujeong Lim raised the possibility that it could affect Pro Max sales going forward:
“Whether China’s outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks. The recovery of US and Japanese volumes, and whether the iPhone Duo launching in Week 43 will generate incremental demand rather than cannibalising Pro Max, are the two most consequential near-term variables.”

articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Oct. 27, 2026: Dow ends flat, S&P 500 logs gains and Nasdaq books best day in nearly a month as chip stocks bounce for a second day and oil prices ease
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 rose on Tuesday as enthusiasm surrounding chipmakers led traders to move into the names for another day. Investors also monitored a slide in oil prices and parsed through a slew of corporate earnings as the Federal Reserve began its two-day policy meeting.
The broad market index was up 0.6% to end at 7,722.60, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 15.99 points, or 0.03%, to close at 52,377.57. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.18% to settle at 26,477.81.
Shares of Broadcom climbed 4% on the heels of a coalition of banks — namely, Bank of America , Citi and Morgan Stanley — and Blackstone announcing $63 billion in financing for the purchase of Broadcom's technology for Anthropic. Other chipmakers rose in sympathy. Micron Technology was up almost 3%, while Advanced Micro Devices gained 5%.
The latest moves in those stocks add to their gains from the prior trading day, which saw the major averages record a winning session , thanks in part to a boost in artificial intelligence-related stocks after Anthropic filed to go public at the Nasdaq. This would mark another major tech IPO for 2026, following SpaceX's blockbuster listing in June.
"The market has these kind of periodic interludes where it gets concerned about AI spending, and then we tend to go back and tech leads us higher," said Jed Ellerbroek, Argent Capital Management portfolio manager. "The light switch has been off for the last two weeks, and it looks like the first two days this week, the switch has been flipped up again."
Despite those recent concerns, Ellerbroek still sees "great" conviction from companies that own data centers to continue to grow. "The potential crack in the foundation remains just how volatile capital markets can be," he added.
A decline in oil prices also supported sentiment Tuesday. The moves came after Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and his top national security official Mohsen Rezaei discussed the country's conditions for ending the conflict. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures settled down 1.83% to $99.90 per barrel, while global benchmark Brent crude futures shed 1.67% to close at $113.88 a barrel.
Meanwhile, JetBlue jumped 19% despite the airline posting a larger-than-expected third-quarter loss, as the company said it expects to see further margin expansion in the fourth quarter. UPS shares added more than 5% after the delivery giant reported better-than-expected results for the third quarter.
The Fed is set to deliver its rate policy decision on Wednesday afternoon. While the central bank is expected to keep rates unchanged, traders will look for clues on whether another rate hike will take place before year-end.
"This feels like a rare Fed meeting non-event under Warsh. It feels like his communication strategy is going to result in fewer of these no-surprise meetings, but it it does look like we're going to get one here, mostly because the midterm election is next week," Ellerbroek also said. "I assume that next meeting in December is going to be another kind of live wire."
The three major averages ended higher on Tuesday.
The S&P 500 gained 0.6% to 7,722.60, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.18% to 26,477.81. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added just 15.99 points, or 0.03%, to 52,377.57.
Bank of America has added SpaceX and Fox Corporation to its U.S. 1 list, which is a collection of the firm's top buy-rated stocks.
SpaceX shares were up nearly 1.2% and shares for Fox Corp were slightly higher on Tuesday morning following the firm's note.
The firm has removed RenaissanceRe Holdings from the US 1 List but maintains the company's buy rating.
Shares of steel producer Nucor are advancing more than 6% Tuesday on the back of a solid third quarter delivered on Monday. The stock is now up 67% year-to-date.
"The demand drivers in the steel-centric side of our economy are booming," Nucor CEO Leon Topalian told CNBC Tuesday, citing strong steel demand from data centers, pharma and natural gas.
The company's revenue of $11.25 billion was well ahead of the estimated $10.84 billion, according to FactSet. Its earnings per share of $5.80 came in ahead of the company's guidance of $5.55-$5.65 but slightly below FactSet's $5.84.
Still, Topalian noted, the company's "demand drivers are stronger than any time I've seen in my 31 years at Nucor."
General Motors will have a new home on the Nasdaq starting Nov. 17. The automaker decided to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange as part of its shift to becoming a more technology-focused company.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release.
The exchange switch will make it eligible for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 Index , the company noted. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain GM.
— Michael Wayland and Michelle Fox
Shares of Constellation Energy are up more than 2% after the Department of Energy offered a $5 billion conditional loan to help upgrade several of the company's nuclear plants.
The loans will help modernize several Constellation plants in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania. The upgrades will squeeze more than a gigawatt of additional electricity out of existing reactors, according to the Department of Energy .
Constellation and Alphabet's Google unit struck a deal earlier this month to modernize 11 nuclear plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Those upgrades will bring 890 megawatts of additional capacity.
Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG, is saying to fade the chip bounce in the artificial intelligence trade.
In October presentation notes, he drew comparisons between current conditions in the SOX semiconductor index and large past down legs.
Looking at times when the index has moved down by 5% following an upward movement of the same magnitude, as the SOX has done recently, Krinsky noted that this phenomenon has only occurred a handful of times over the past 30 years.
"There have only been four prior occurrences. Three were in July – Sep. '95, and one was March 17th, 2000. The former led to a - 53% drawdown while the latter was the dead peak of the dot-com bubble top leading to a -83% decline," he wrote.
Consumer confidence improved in October as gasoline prices moved lower and the outlook for employment brightened a bit, according to a survey released Tuesday.
The Conference Board's monthly indicator posted a reading of 91.7, up 7.5 points from September and better than the forecast for 81 from the Dow Jones consensus. Indexes measuring the present situation and expectations also saw gains.
"The recovery was in line with retail gasoline prices easing from September to October. Yet, despite the increase in October, consumer confidence remained on the long-term downward trend that's persisted over the past few years," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.
Gas prices are off nearly 20 cents a gallon from their late-September readings, according to the Energy Information Administration.
On employment, the gap between respondents indicating that jobs are "plentiful" against "hard to get" narrowed by 2.4 percentage points to 5.3 points.
Stephens is initiating coverage on Mama's Creations with an overweight rating.
The firm put a $19 price target for the company, implying a 55% upside from Monday's close.
"MAMA has evolved from a single-brand meatball company into a scaled deli solutions platform, with three manufacturing facilities and a portfolio spanning beef, chicken, salads, olives and sides," wrote analyst Jim Salera.

articles.content_orig:
United Parcel Service on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlook last quarter . UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion.
Shares of UPS rose slightly in morning trading.
Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69. Revenue rose 6.7% to $22.9 billion.
In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment had a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, including healthcare . On a call with analysts, CEO Carol Tomé said healthcare revenue exceeded $3 billion for the third consecutive quarter.
The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down with Amazon .
"We're driving more premium growth, improving revenue quality and mix, and creating greater operating leverage through a more efficient network," Tomé said on the call. "All of this is strengthening the underlying performance of our business."
UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth.
As the company prepares for its peak holiday season, Tomé said the consumer remains resilient, and the growth in average daily volume between the third and fourth quarters will be consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume is expected to fall due to the reduction with Amazon.
She added that nearly 70% of all packages will flow through an automated process this holiday season.

articles.title_orig: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.title_zh: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
In the first mega IPO of 2026, SpaceX ( SPCX ) singled out one person in its prospectus as the shot caller: none other than the world's richest person, Elon Musk.
The next big IPO of the year — Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), which could be the largest of all time — is run more by a committee of founders. That's a good thing given its mission and structures, according to veteran dealmaker Jim Neeson.
"I would say having seven founders working together can make it where it's not just like a cult of Elon Musk, right?" the Connor Group founding executive said on Sozzi Unleashed . "You actually have it where you have a consortium of people making decisions, which I actually think can be a good thing."
Neeson noted that Anthropic is a public benefit company with seven founders who collectively own 50.1%.
"You have a board that will be approved by sort of a trust fund. And then you also have a business where it's not just going to be about profits. It's also going to be sort of the social benefit piece that's built into their doctrine," he explained.
Anthropic's founders are CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and president, Daniela Amodei, as well as Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah. The consortium left OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) to start Anthropic in January 2021.
The seven co-founders will be issued new Class F common stock as part of the IPO, giving them majority control of the company — something Neeson said investors will have to navigate.
"If you look at Meta, [and] you also look at Google, you had very strong founders," Neeson said. "A lot of times that is the venture capital case. I want founders that can make strong decisions and not be beholden to sort of quarterly type of trends."
"This is going to be a different type of structure out there, and it's going to be tested," he added. "We've never seen it, especially at this scale, especially at these growth rates. So I would say that's one thing analysts and investors are going to be looking very closely at."
The group looks to be managing the financials relatively well.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus showed. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
On an adjusted basis, Anthropic posted $1.62 billion in operating income through the first six months of 2026 compared to a loss of $1.85 billion last year.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Brent holds near $115 as Iran war tensions and escalating Saudi-Houthi hostilities keep oil markets on edge ahead of U.S. midterms.
Hormuz Becomes Even More Dangerous — and More Expensive
- October has seen the most acute escalation in maritime attacks since the US-Iran war started eight months ago, with already more than 30 incidents recorded in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways, up from 14 in September.
- The most recent addition to the list of maritime targets is a crude tanker in Iraq's exclusive economic zone, signaling that it is not only tankers seeking to surreptitiously transit the Hormuz that get targeted by Iran.
- VLCCs, the largest crude tankers available, account for 28% of all drone and missile attacks in the Persian Gulf, with the 32 impacted ships representing almost 4% of the global VLCC fleet.
- Freight rates from the Gulf remain elevated with a Saudi Arabia-China voyage still costing around $33 per barrel, whilst regional demurrage rates have been rising since mid-August to their current level of $1,000,000/day.
- UKMTO, a provider of maritime security alerts, recently admitted that it is becoming increasingly more difficult to report on strikes as transiting ships prefer to sail unnoticed and charterers are wary of pushing freight rates even higher.
- US gas producer EQT (NYSE:EQT) has agreed to buy Range Resources (NYSE:RRC) in a $13 billion all-stock deal to create the largest US gas company, with the combined Appalachian-focused company having a net output of more than 9 bcf/d.
- US energy firm Ovintiv (NYSE:OVV) will acquire Canada's Logan Energy in an all-cash deal valued at $0.9 billion, adding around 20,000 boe/d of production and 266,000 net acres across the Montney shale play.
- UK oil major BP (NYSE:BP) has started the second phase of exploration in Venezuela's offshore Loran gas field, using the research and survey vessel Fugro Brasilis to perform final seabed studies.
- US oil giant ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) reported a commercial discovery with its Rockhead-1 exploration well offshore Guyana, its first drilling success since the 2024 Hatchetfish find with a resource estimate of 500-600 million barrels.
- Italian oil major ENI (BIT:ENI) has launched the construction of its 3 TCf Cronos project offshore Cyprus, aiming for first gas in the first half of 2028, to be exported via Egypt's Damietta LNG terminal. Tuesday, October 27, 2026
The oil markets are counting down the days until the November 3 midterm elections in the US, with expectations of impending hostilities rising into next month. Last-minute efforts to negotiate some form of de-escalation are ongoing, with both Qatar and Pakistan seeking to mediate between the Trump administration and Tehran, temporarily capping the upside for ICE Brent at $115 per barrel. Simultaneously to Hormuz tensions, the Saudi-Houthi conflict appears to be gaining self-sustaining momentum.
OPEC+ Holds the Fort on Supply Hikes. OPEC+ is expected to hold December output targets steady at its Sunday's meeting, with seven core members focusing on 2027 production quotas instead after they've completed the roll-back of 1.65 million b/d voluntary cuts, disrupted by the Hormuz crisis.
US Moves China Shipping Fees into 2027. The US is considering extending its truce with China on port charges for Chinese-linked ships by two months to January 9, preserving a suspension of tit-for-tat fees that previously imposed millions of dollars per port call and raised freight costs.
Houthis Hit Saudi Arabia's Largest Refinery. Yemen's Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike hit Saudi Arabia's 550,000 b/d Ras Tanura refinery, causing a fire and disrupting operations at the Middle Eastern kingdom's largest plant, with an earlier March attack shutting it for three months.
Refining Boom Derails Galp–Moeve Merger. Portugal's Galp and Spain's Moeve have abandoned plans for a potential downstream merger that would've combined 700,000 b/d of refining capacity and 3,500 service stations, claiming that 2026 bumper profits made it harder to agree M&A terms.
Brussels Builds a European Wall Against China. The European Union may introduce quotas or tariffs on Chinese chemicals, furniture and machinery from early 2027, seeking to replicate its recent import caps on hybrid vehicles as it struggles to narrow its €360 billion trade deficit.
Singapore Launches First LNG Term Tender. Singapore's state gas buyer GasCo launched its first ever LNG term supply tender after neighbouring Indonesia had announced it would slash pipeline gas exports by 15% to 31 MMCf/d , just as the government plans to add 5 new gas-powered plants.
East Timor Buys Out Its Untapped Offshore Gem. Australia's major Woodside (ASX:WDS) has agreed to sell its stakes in the Greater Sunrise fields offshore East Timor for $200 million to the island nation, leaving state oil firm Timor gap as the only stakeholder of the untapped 5.3 TCf field.
Alberta Pushes for Scrapping of Tanker Ban. The province of Alberta called on the Carney government to repeal Canada's 2019 West Coast tanker ban that bars vessels carrying over 12,500 tonnes from loading at British Columbia ports, backing a proposed 250,000 b/d crude-by-rail route.
Indonesia Gives Up on Market-Based Imports. Indonesia plans to replace tender-based crude oil and refined product imports with government-to-government (G2G) and government-to-business (G2B) agreements to secure supplies, courting India and China for long-term supply deals.
Dangote Considers Third African Refinery. Nigeria's Dangote conglomerate is considering building a third 700,000 b/d refinery in Africa, alongside the existing plant in Lekki and the upcoming Kenyan refinery in Lamu, whilst simultaneously investing into refined product pipelines in West Africa.
Malaysia Doubles Down on Coal. The Malaysia government has proposed extending the lifespan of its existing coal-fuelled power plants despite an earlier pledge to retire coal by 2044, with coal accounting for 56% of current generation as JKM prices jumped to $33 per MMBtu this week.
Iron Ore Plunges Again on China Demand Fears. Iron ore prices fell to their lowest since September 2024 as weak Chinese demand and wafer-thin margins are expected to curb Q4 steel consumption, sending the Dalian iron ore futures to ¥662 per tonne, below the $100 per tonne threshold. White House to Ease Methane Emission Rules. The Trump administration is planning to relax rules on methane emissions from oil and gas operations, including exemptions for wells producing up to 15 boe/d, projecting incremental output of 210 million barrels for older and depleted wells.
Bahri Orders Three New VLCCs to Expand Tanker Fleet. Saudi national shipping company Bahri has ordered three VLCCs from domestic shipbuilder International Maritime Industries for $451 million, with deliveries scheduled in 2029-30 and marking the first attempt at exclusively Saudi shipbuilding.
UK Considers Fast-Track Approvals for Tiebacks. The UK's Burnham government is considering the fast-tracking of a small number of oil and gas tiebacks before pending legislation creates Transitional Energy Certificates that extend existing fields but preserve the country's exploration ban.

articles.title_orig: Dutch zookeeper dies after leopard attacked her in the animal’s enclosure
articles.title_zh: Dutch zookeeper dies after leopard attacked her in the animal’s enclosure
articles.content_orig:
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

articles.title_orig: US’s RFK Jr claims Arabs ‘don’t produce science’: Why he’s very, very wrong
articles.title_zh: US’s RFK Jr claims Arabs ‘don’t produce science’: Why he’s very, very wrong
articles.content_orig:
United States Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has sparked uproar with comments he has made denying Arab contributions to mathematics, science and literature.
In a high-voltage rant on Monday, the US health secretary said, “There’s five hundred million Arabs in the world. And yet they don’t produce science. They don’t win the Nobel Prize. They don’t win the Fields Prize. They don’t win the Wolf Prize. They don’t produce literature.”
RFK Jr, who has been involved in anti-vaccine campaigns and has promoted a debunked theory linking vaccines to autism, made the comments during a US election campaign event in Grand Rapids, Michigan while supporting Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who is up against Arab-American Democrat nominee Abdul El-Sayed, in a tightly contested battle for Michigan’s Senate seat in next week’s midterm elections.
Critics said the comments were racist, Islamophobic and factually inaccurate, pointing to modern and historic Arab innovation in multiple fields.
Here’s how Arabs have made vital contributions to the human understanding of maths, science and literature through the centuries.
The period known as the Islamic Golden Age, from around 750 AD to 1258 AD, produced many key Arab contributions to medicine at a time when Europe was said to be in its Dark Ages. During this time, Arabic was the language of science and scholarship.
1st-4th centuries: The numerals 0-9, which originated in ancient India, were adopted by Arab mathematicians who spread them across the world. They displaced Roman numerals as a more advanced number system in mathematics.
8th century: Arab and Persian mathematicians were studying the ancient Indian concept of zero in mathematics in Baghdad, long before the Europeans. The number zero was crucial to the development of mathematics – but was absent from widely used Roman numerals in Europe.
813-833: The Arab mathematician Muḥammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi – one of those studying the number 0 – is often referred to as the “father of algebra” as he was the first to treat the method as a separate mathematical discipline in his work, Al-Jabr. This method provided the first linear and quadratic equations, still used as a core part of mathematical study today.
965-1040: Ibn al-Haytham, known as the “father of modern optics”, explained the role that light entering the eye plays in human vision. He was born in Basra in Iraq, but spent most of his working life in Cairo attending to noble families.
936-1013: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, called “the father of modern surgery”, was considered the greatest surgeon in the Middle Ages. He wrote a 30-volume encyclopaedia detailing medical practices and designed and illustrated many surgical instruments. Born in Azahara, in Andalusia, he was known as Abulcasis in Europe.
9th century: Fatima al-Fihri founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco. It is often cited as the oldest continually operating university.
1213-1288: Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation – the process by which blood passes through the lungs – several centuries before Europeans understood it. He wrote more than 110 volumes of work on surgery, ophthalmology and philosophy while working as a chief physician in Egypt.
915-965: Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, regarded as the greatest poet in the Arabic language, was Yemeni and grew up immersed in Bedouin Arabic culture. He wrote in classical Arabic and many of his verses became sayings used in everyday Arabic.
1100-1165: Muhammad al-Idrisi was a geographer known for making the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most accurate and detailed medieval world maps, and a high point of Islamic geography. He was born in Ceuta in Morocco.
In more modern times, RFK Jr’s assertion that Arabs do not win Nobel prizes for science and literature is very far from the truth. Here are some of the highlights:
Peter Medawar won the Nobel Prize for Medicine for work on for work on acquired immune tolerance, which underpins organ transplantation. He was born in Brazil to a Lebanese father.
Michael Atiyah won the Fields Medal, the most prestigious award for mathematics, in 1966. He was born in London to a Lebanese father and Scottish mother. Educated in Egypt, he spent much of his childhood in Cairo and Khartoum.
Egyptian Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his body of work, including the Cairo Trilogy, which the Swedish Academy said formed “an Arabic narrative art that applies to all mankind”. He is still the only winner of the prize who wrote in Arabic.
Elias James Corey won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for developing retrosynthetic analysis. He is an American of Lebanese descent.
Egyptian Ahmed Zewail won the Wolf Prize for Chemistry. The Wolf Prize is an international award which has been presented to living scientists and artists every year in Israel by the Wolf Foundation since 1978.
Zewail also won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for pioneering femtochemistry, which is the study of chemical reactions on extremely short timescales. He also won the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1993.
Egyptian scientist Mohamed ElBaradei shared his Nobel Prize with the International Atomic Energy Agency, which he led.
Omar M Yaghi,  born in Jordan to a Palestinian refugee family, won the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2018 for work on metal-organic frameworks. He shared the prize with Japan’s Makoto Fujita. The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) condemned his acceptance of the award because the prize is awarded by an Israeli foundation.
Moungi Bawendi won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots. He was born in France to a Tunisian father, but based in the US.
Yaghi also won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for developing metal-organic frameworks. These are crystalline materials with large internal cavities that can capture and store gases, harvest water from air, and trap pollutants. He shared the prize with Susumu Kitagawa from Japan and Richard Robson from Australia.
In a post on X, vaccine scientist Peter Hotez of the Texas Medical Center weighed in on historical Arab scholarship, saying, “It was the Arab scientists of the Middle Ages who kept Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen alive to hand it down in the Renaissance.”
Broadcaster Mehdi Hasan described RFK Jr’s comments as “racist” and, in a post on X, wrote: “One of the men who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry last year was a Palestinian-American, Omar Yaghi.”
The Council on American-Islamic Relations called for the US health secretary to be removed. It said: “To stand on a public stage as a sitting US cabinet official and dehumanise half a billion people – and millions of Muslim and Christian Arab Americans – with fabricated, white supremacist talking points is utterly disqualifying for public office. His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.”

articles.title_orig: Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Stock Will Go Parabolic on Oct. 30
articles.title_zh: Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Stock Will Go Parabolic on Oct. 30
articles.content_orig:
As technology companies race to build data centers, demand for the memory chips that make artificial intelligence (AI) computing possible has skyrocketed. One of the leading manufacturers of memory chips for AI hyperscalers is Micron Technology ( MU +2.77% ) .
So far this year, Micron stock has soared 225% -- making it the third-highest performer in the Nasdaq-100. Nevertheless, Micron's shares have experienced considerable volatility over the last couple of months and trade about 24% below their all-time high.
I think this disconnect is about to reverse. On Oct. 28 and 29, Alphabet ( GOOGL +1.19% ) ( GOOG +0.84% ) and Amazon ( AMZN +1.61% ) are scheduled to report quarterly earnings. While investors will undoubtedly focus on their respective AI-related capital expenditures (capex), I think another topic could emerge as a major discussion point: the global memory shortage. If my prediction is accurate, Micron could begin to rally just in time for Halloween.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/27/26
For most of the AI revolution, investors primarily associated infrastructure with graphics processing units (GPUs) designed by Nvidia and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) designed by Broadcom . However, GPUs and custom silicon cannot operate efficiently without sufficient memory. Micron manufactures dynamic random access memory (DRAM) and high bandwidth memory (HBM), both of which are critical components of the AI chip stack.
Interestingly, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy already highlighted the growing importance of memory during the company's last earnings call. Jassy explained that Amazon planned to increase its 2026 capex budget to $220 billion -- up from its previous forecast of $200 billion -- specifically because of higher memory costs.
Meanwhile, Alphabet raised its 2026 capex forecast to $195 billion to $205 billion during its second-quarter earnings call. Management attributed the increase to accelerating infrastructure investments and capacity supply constraints. Although Alphabet did not explicitly identify memory as the culprit, its comments reinforce the underlying idea that demand for AI compute is insatiable.
As both companies prepare to report earnings this week, investors should pay close attention to any additional commentary surrounding memory availability, pricing, and infrastructure spending.
Image source: Getty Images.
Amazon and Alphabet aren't the only companies confronting the memory shortage. Earlier this month, Elon Musk took to X (formerly Twitter) to discuss the bottlenecks facing AI infrastructure build-outs. Musk specifically identified RAM supply as a constraint, supporting the idea that memory availability is becoming just as important as access to advanced processors.
This distinction matters because the AI infrastructure boom is moving beyond simply procuring as many GPUs as possible. AI models need memory to support training and inference. Training involves teaching AI to recognize patterns , while inference occurs when those models are deployed to perform an actual task rather than just answer a query. Both activities require substantial memory, particularly as applications become more complex across autonomous systems, robotics, and agentic AI.
A prolonged memory shortage could create favorable conditions for Micron. When demand for a product exceeds available supply, manufacturers can command higher prices . For Micron, this is already happening and translating into accelerating revenue growth, expanding profit margins, and earnings visibility.
MU Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts
One of the biggest headwinds dragging on Micron stock right now is skepticism about the semiconductor industry's boom-and-bust cycles and whether hyperscalers can maintain the pace of their infrastructure spending. I think Amazon's and Alphabet's upcoming earnings reports will help answer that question.
If leadership explicitly emphasizes the memory shortage, rising component prices, or the increasing demand for memory-intensive AI applications, investors may begin to view Micron's growth as more durable than anticipated.
My prediction is that earnings season will become a turning point for Micron stock. If the world's largest AI developers stress the industry's memory shortage, investors should recognize that Micron's opportunity extends well beyond this year. With shares still trading meaningfully below their all-time high, positive commentary could provide a much-needed catalyst for a new rally.
