Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results on deck from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
United Parcel Service ( UPS ) stock rose 2% on Tuesday after the courier posted third quarter results and raised its full-year guidance, signaling solid demand during the upcoming holiday season.
Revenue is expected to come in at $92.6 billion this year, up from a prior forecast of $91.2 billion. UPS also increased its adjusted earnings guidance.
Despite inflation pressures and high diesel costs, UPS is optimistic heading into the last few months of the year.
"US consumers remain resilient and the outlook for holiday demand is strong," CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call.
The company is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan aimed at cost-cutting and reconfiguring its delivery network.
JetBlue Airways ( JBLU ) shares rose more than 14% in premarket trading on Tuesday following the release of third-quarter results and guidance for 2027. The airline reported a loss per share of $0.60, compared to analyst estimates of $0.54. Revenue reached $2.81 billion, slightly below the $2.83 billion consensus estimate.
The airline posted an operating margin of negative 5.1% for the quarter. Operating revenue totaled $2.81 billion while operating expenses came in at $2.96 billion. The company's operating revenue increased 21% year-over-year.
Chief Executive Officer Joanna Geraghty said resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue ahead of initial expectations, allowing the company to offset more of the fuel cost increases than anticipated. She noted that Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver strong results even as the company grows capacity in that market.
Yahoo Finance's Brooke DiPalma reports:
Coca-Cola ( KO ) posted better-than-expected third quarter results and raised its earnings outlook, but the company saw slowing demand in its North American business.
Coca-Cola stock traded lower in early trading.
The company posted adjusted earnings of $0.91 per share, above the $0.88 expected by Wall Street analysts, alongside revenue of $13.4 billion, also higher than estimates of $12.9 billion.
Overall unit case volume grew by 5%, more than the roughly 3% expected. The increase was once again led by Coke Zero, which grew roughly 16% year over year. Diet Coke and Coca-Cola Light grew by 6%.
Boeing ( BA ) shrank its quarterly losses and generated cash flow in the third quarter, but its top- and bottom-line results missed Wall Street's expectations.
Revenue of $24.1 billion and an adjusted loss per share of $0.34 came in below estimates of revenue of $24.3 billion and a loss of $0.20 per share.
The company's commercial airplane unit faced higher costs in its supply chain and for production as well as a $700 million charge on its 777X program. As a result, its operating margin in that segment fell to -6.5%.
"Backlog reached a record $745B. The 737-7 and 737-10 FAA certifications and F/A-XX award are meaningful milestones, though BCA margin deterioration to -6.5% from Q2's -2.7% introduces uncertainty around the recovery pace," CFRA analysts wrote in a note following the results.
SoFi ( SOFI ) stock surged 10% in premarket trading on Tuesday after the online financial services provider lifted its 2026 outlook and reported strong results for the third quarter.
Here's what SoFi reported for Q3, compared to Wall Street analyst estimates compiled by S&P Market Intelligence:
Revenue: up 45.9% year over year to $1.39 billion, above estimates of $1.26 billion.
Adjusted earnings: $0.18, above estimates of $0.17.
Updated 2026 guidance: SoFi now expects net revenue of $5.04 billion in 2026, reflecting a 40% year-over-year increase. Adjusted EBITDA is now expected at $1.66 billion of adjusted EBITDA, and earnings per share are forecast at $0.61. Wall Street analysts were expecting 2026 earnings per share of $0.59.
The company also introduced 2027 guidance, guiding for $0.90 of earnings per share, which is above the Street's estimate of $ 0.82.
"We had exceptional Q3 results against the backdrop of any environment, but they are even more remarkable given how 2026 has unfolded," CEO Anthony Noto said. "Our focus is simple. We are adding more members, who are using more products, and generating more revenue per product to create the most value for our shareholders over the long run. In less than a decade, we have transformed SoFi from a single-product company into an everything financial app with eight different businesses each generating over $100 million in annualized revenue."
Whirlpool posted another mixed quarter as inflation and lower demand in North America took a toll.
"What is new and different is the increasingly inflationary environment that has happened from Q2 into Q3, as well as the impact of volume deleveraging which is driven by the softer demand that we have in the North America industry," Whirlpool CFO Roxanne Warner told Yahoo Finance, adding that the team is focusing on what it can control.
In the third quarter, the company reported revenue declined by nearly 9% to $3.68 billion, which was below estimates of $3.91 billion. The company reported an adjusted loss per share of $0.21, lower than the adjusted earnings per share estimate of $0.76,  per Bloomberg consensus data
Warner said that the industry hasn't caught up to the "full impact of the inflationary pressures from 2022," with inflation up 12% since then.
For that reason,  the company plans to raise prices for the third time this year, now by 7% in the fourth quarter. That follows its largest price increase in history in April, at 10%, and a 4% increase in its list prices in July.
Revenue for major appliances in its North America business fell 8.3% year over year to $2.5 billion, below Wall Street's expectations.
Whirlpool's small domestic appliance business fell almost 1% to $286 million, below the expected $314 million. However, the company said that in the third quarter, some items sold out, leading to roughly 40% year-over-year growth in US orders in October.

articles.title_orig: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.title_zh: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.content_orig:
Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

articles.title_orig: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war
articles.title_zh: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

articles.title_orig: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.title_zh: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.content_orig:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.
We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?
In Serbia and Brazil, huge numbers of voters turned out on Sunday to repudiate right-wing populists.
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .
Vox isn’t typically in the business of covering elections in far-flung locales like the central Balkans. (No offense whatsoever to anyone from the central Balkans!) But on Sunday, an insurgent student-backed movement in Serbia successfully toppled the country’s ruling right-wing political machine, creating an unexpected opening for democratic reform.
Then, in another upset halfway around the globe, Brazilian voters reelected incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro. “Democracy always, dictatorship never again,” Lula said in his victory speech.
That’s two big repudiations of the nationalist right in 24 hours. Not quite enough to declare a trend, maybe, but sufficient to remind us that there’s still hope for the world’s embattled democratic institutions.
More than that, these results offer evidence of something that sounds naive and Pollyannish in our current moment, but can (apparently!) still prove true: Organizing can be a powerful force for electoral change — both abroad and maybe here at home.
To be fair, the two elections differed considerably, and I don’t want to suggest it’s all sunshine and democratic renewal ahead for Brazil and Serbia. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, for instance. And in Serbia, the victorious Student List still has to stand up a government, a prime minister, and a full policy platform — something the nascent movement has never done before.
But academics and elections-watchers in both countries have credited the results in large part to mass protests and grassroots organizing that helped mobilize unexpected numbers of voters .
Serbian students began their movement in 2024, following the partial collapse of a railway station that killed 16 people. The government’s failure to fully explain the cause of the collapse — or hold anyone responsible — fueled months of marches, protest bike rides, and other demonstrations. That movement eventually grew into the Student List: an opposition electoral slate that fielded 250 candidates in Sunday’s parliamentary elections.
The story in Brazil is quite different. Lula, the country’s leftist president, was actually poised to lose. Brazil uses a two-round popular vote to elect its president, and if no candidate secures more than half the vote in the first round, then the top two candidates proceed to a runoff election. Lula placed second in that first vote, after Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and the heir to his father’s far-right political movement.
To many Brazilians, that second-place finish served as a kind of wake-up call. “No runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media,” Guilherme Casarões , an associate professor of Brazilian studies at Florida International University, wrote in an analysis of the surprise results. One WhatsApp channel dedicated to turning voters out for Lula grew to nearly 11 million followers , up from just 50,000 after his first-round loss.
Looking at these projects abroad, I’m struck that American pro-democracy movements like No Kings haven’t achieved that kind of influence. Arguably, that’s in part a consequence of their failure to turn protest energy into actual political organizing — things like registering voters, knocking on doors, and fielding candidates.
But there are some signs that may be shifting. No Kings has lately pivoted its focus, for instance, from mostly organizing protests to urging Americans — of both parties — to vote in the midterms. And Indivisible, one of the groups behind the movement, claims that early voting surged during the latest protests in the zip codes where they occurred.
It’s not exactly a central Balkan moment, but maybe it’s a hint of things to come. Elections can surprise you, after all. Just ask a Serb or a Brazilian.
➨ Leave your big life decisions to chance. (Sort of.) A team of researchers invited people to make a big life decision by flipping a coin and then tracked their happiness with the outcome. They found that, of the people who obeyed the results of the toss, the ones who changed something big were overwhelmingly happier. That doesn’t literally mean we should all resort to coin tosses, but it should tell us something important: We often tend to be too cautious about making major changes .

articles.title_orig: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.title_zh: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
We are only two days into the week, and it already feels like it should be the weekend.
In the past two days, Meta ( META ) said it will raise $95 billion to support its AI build-out through stock offerings, and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) dropped a 407-page IPO prospectus that I know you haven't read in its entirety. (Wall Street hasn't either, so don't lose sleep over it.)
Lost in that activity is that earnings season continues in full swing, with results from Coca-Cola ( KO ), Hilton ( HLT ), UPS ( UPS ), Whirlpool ( WHR ), and others today.
While investors are jacked up about AI and some stability returning to the tech trade, don't lose sight of earnings season: After all, it's earnings and earnings expectations that power stocks, not Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (although his comments have moved markets in the past).
So here are a few quick takes on a couple of earnings reports I chewed through this morning:
I don't have any problems with this Hilton quarter, even though the stock is getting hit on a slight revenue miss. The important revenue per available room metric grew 5.8%, the company remains an aggressive buyer of its stock, and it approved the development of 30,500 rooms in the quarter.
The report fits nicely with the Delta ( DAL ) report we got last week, in that higher fuel prices don't appear to be slowing leisure or business travelers.
I think it also fits nicely with the numbers out of UPS today, with US sales up 4.5% and its full-year guidance hike.
Coca-Cola's latest guidance lift reinforces the view that the company continues to take massive market share away from rival PepsiCo ( PEP ). Coke Zero sales surged 16%.
Not a good day for the team at PepsiCo up in Purchase, N.Y.
I continue to be absolutely shocked by what's happening at Whirlpool ( WHR ). Another supersoft quarter, with an adjusted loss of $0.21 per share. Costs are up, and the business is being hurt by a near-frozen US housing market.
You need nerves of steel to buy Whirlpool shares here — the stock is down more than 63% this year. If you do, the thesis has to be that the iconic company is acquired at some point in the next 12 months.

articles.title_orig: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.title_zh: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has devised an unusual way for its founders to pass on their power.
In its IPO filings , Anthropic outlined how seven of its cofounders, who collectively have 50.1% of voting control, will be able to create a ranked list of who they'd like to inherit their power in the event of their death or incapacitation.
What's particularly notable is that while the names would be shared with the other LLC members and Anthropic's Nominating Committee, they are otherwise contractually confidential and generally not public.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , Anthropic President Daniela Amodei, and the five other LLC members will review and vote on whether to approve their fellow founders' proposed successors, but the names will likely never be seen by other shareholders. (The agreement allows for the publication only in narrow circumstances, such as a court order or other legal requirement.)
Under the agreement, which was first highlighted by Forbes , each member of the Founders LLC may name up to 10 potential successors, ranked in order of preference. The other LLC members must then vote to approve the secret lists.
While succession plans are not unusual, Anthropic's approach is unusual in how it ranks potential successors. It also underscores how, thanks to the Founders LLC, Anthropic's leaders will be able to maintain control as shareholders begin to offer input post-IPO.
Facebook's 2012 IPO paperwork suggested that if Mark Zuckerberg were in control of the company at the time of his death, then control could be transferred to someone he designated. (Meta has since tweaked this plan.) In 2020, Airbnb's three cofounders agreed to transfer their voting power to their other cofounders if one of them died or became disabled, but that arrangement (which still exists) only lasts for nine months.
The succession plan does not establish CEO succession. Anthropic's board of directors would handle such a chief executive appointment.
There are also some limitations to who the Anthropic founders can name on their lists.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Eight of their 10 potential successors are subject to eligibility requirements, including that the person named is a current or former employee of Anthropic or one of its subsidiaries, or has worked for "a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization or a national or international organization whose primary purpose is research, education, or the promotion of public benefit." In either case, the person must have worked there for at least three years.
If the person worked for Anthropic, they must have held a specific role, such as a member of the technical staff or the company's internal think tank, or another role approved by the board and a majority of the other members. If they worked outside Anthropic, they must have held a senior role at the nonprofit. These successors must also be US citizens, have permanent residency, or have valid work authorization.
The other two names, if a founder names all 10 potential successors, are not subject to the eligibility requirements, but they must also receive the required approval.
The succession plan doesn't last forever.
Under the agreement, a successor member generally would cease to be a member on the 10th anniversary of Anthropic's IPO. After that point, successor designees may be admitted only in limited circumstances during a transition period.

articles.title_orig: Apple hit by ‘Crackgate’ outcry over iPhone Duo screen problems
articles.title_zh: Apple hit by ‘Crackgate’ outcry over iPhone Duo screen problems
articles.content_orig:
Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for preorders.
But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.
Apple on Monday said that it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."
Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out of warranty.
Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forums such as Reddit and X , and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design.
"Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari in its teardown video . "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently."
"The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens posted on X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."
Breaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, and reviewers quickly found that its inner screen cracked during normal use.
Early reviewers praised the experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.
Apple said Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device.
"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Federal Reserve kicked off its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers who nevertheless seem reluctant to hike rates this month.
Fed watchers expect the central bank to keep benchmark rates in the 3.75% to 4% range , with bond traders pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike on Wednesday, per CME Group. A rate hike in December appears far more likely, however, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , several officials' remarks suggest the Fed will hold rates this month to continue assessing additional data. The proximity of the October meeting to the US midterm elections next Tuesday is also seen as a deterrent to bold monetary policy moves.
With the Fed holding rates steady seen as all but given, the focus is on what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will say at his post-FOMC-meeting press conference on Wednesday. Warsh has deliberately avoided telegraphing future Fed policy moves, but hot inflation could elicit more insight from him into the path forward.
The Federal Open Market Committee's two-day policy meeting has started and will conclude at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The FOMC's decision on whether to cut, hold, or raise interest rates will be released at 2 p.m. tomorrow. Following that decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. that will be live-streamed.
This is the seventh FOMC meeting this year. The final Fed meeting of the year will take place from Dec. 8-9 and will include a Summary of Economic Projections, which will be used to gauge where policymakers see rates heading in 2027.
The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections.
Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause."
Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity.
"This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike."
The Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting kicked off this morning at 9:30 a.m. ET, as scheduled, a Fed spokesperson confirmed.
Expectations remain firm that the Fed will hold rates steady in a range of 3.75% to 4% after hiking by 25 basis points in September. Traders broadly view that the Fed will hike again in December.
But in October, there's a strong belief the Fed won't move rates. According to CME Group's FedWatch, traders see a 90% chance of no move.

Announcing third-quarter 2026 financial results before the market opened today, Corning (NYSE:GLW) provided investors with a lot to celebrate. With shares of the specialized glass manufacturer dipping lower this morning, though, it's clear that investors weren't impressed with the company's recent performance.
As of 1:08 p.m., ET, Corning shares are down 1%, paring back an earlier loss of 4.7%.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images.
Corning reported revenue of $436 million for its solar business in Q3 2026, a quarter-over-quarter decrease from the $438 million it reported in Q2 2026. In addition, Corning reported a $7 million net loss for its solar business, consistent with the $7 million net loss it incurred in Q2 2026 and a sharper loss from the same period in 2025, when it reported $30 million in net income for its solar business.
In the Q2 2026 earnings presentation, management stated that the solar business's revenue and profitability would improve in Q3.
Reporting Q3 2026 core sales of $5.08 billion, Corning beat analysts' expectations of $5.03 billion. At the bottom of the income statement, the company reported Q3 core earnings per share (EPS) of $0.91 -- better than the $0.88 that analysts had anticipated.
Corning manufactures specialized glass, ceramics, and optical materials for numerous applications, including smartphone screens, televisions, telecommunications networks, automotive emissions systems, and laboratory equipment.
For the fourth quarter, Corning projects sales growth of about 19% year over year and EPS growth of 36% year over year.
Investors may find the drop in the solar business disconcerting, but given the company's otherwise strong quarter, it's certainly reasonable to consider picking up shares. articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long discusses the Federal Reserve's upcoming interest rate decisions.
The Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest interest rate decision on Wednesday with the midterm elections less than a week away.
Policymakers at the Fed say they avoid letting politics influence their monetary policy moves, and can be hesitant to hike or cut interest rates at meetings that occur ahead of the election.
Inflation has remained stubbornly high and the September consumer price index (CPI) data showed inflation rose faster than expected, with headline CPI rising 0.6% on a monthly basis and 3.7% from a year ago. The latter figure is well above the central bank's 2% inflation target.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told FOX Business in an interview that while the September inflation data was hotter than expected and raised the prospects of an October rate hike, the Fed is likely to wait to "hike again in December."
CONSUMER INFLATION ROSE FASTER THAN EXPECTED IN SEPTEMBER, CPI REPORT SHOWS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and policymakers are expected to hold rates steady this week. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"This hotter than expected inflation data did increase the chance of an October rate hike , but it's a very high bar to increase in October, they would do it within a week of the election. I know they like to say that they're not political, but it's a high bar for October," she explained.
"Right now, this data indicates that the Fed needs to act again, but it's not a five-alarm fire. They don't have to act immediately, they could wait until December."
"The reality is, gas prices have come down a little bit since the September highs, so we would expect the October data – you know, it won't be great, but it could be a little bit cooler than what we're seeing today. And the Fed has a reasonable case to say, we're probably still gonna hike, but let's wait a few more weeks and see just how broad-based this problem really is," Long said.
FEDERAL RESERVE HIKES INTEREST RATES FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2023 AMID STUBBORN INFLATION
The market expects the Fed to hold rates steady this week, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 90.6% probability of rates remaining at their current target range of 3.75% to 4% – up from 84.5% a week ago and 35.8% last month.
For the Fed's meeting in mid-December, the tool shows a 75.1% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike, which could mark the resumption of the rate-hiking cycle if inflation remains elevated.
WHY THE FED ISN'T READY TO DECLARE VICTORY ON INFLATION
Inflation rose faster than expected in September and remains well above the central bank's 2% target. (Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images)
"The Federal Reserve will definitely hike interest rates again, probably in December," Long said. "The big question is how many more times do they have to hike after that? And what was scary in this latest inflation data for September is to see so many areas of hot inflation: to see used car prices, airfares, recreation costs, auto repair costs, buying a used car, medical costs."
"The story really is starting to take shape that it's probably going to take a couple more hikes in 2027, and this higher-for-longer borrowing costs and mortgage rates well above 7% is going to stick around for at least a year, maybe longer," Long said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CME FedWatch tool shows the market is anticipating multiple rate hikes by March, with a 46.5% chance that rates will be 50 basis points higher than they are now at a range of 4.25% to 4.5%.

articles.title_orig: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.title_zh: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

articles.title_orig: US Army looks to high-flying balloons to help see, strike along front lines with China
articles.title_zh: US Army looks to high-flying balloons to help see, strike along front lines with China
articles.content_orig:
To burst China’s anti-access/area-denial bubble, the U.S. Army is looking at using high-flying balloons with payloads that can monitor the battlefield, relay communications and strike adversaries.
The Army has tinkered with high-altitude balloons for some time, but interest and experimentation have grown in recent years. Against China’s growing arsenal in the vastness of the Pacific , those balloons could provide a cheaper, lower-signature platform that can be employed from dispersed positions, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, commander of the Army’s 7th Infantry Division/Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, or MDC-P, said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C., earlier this month.
Harrington’s command was recently established to merge the ground-maneuver elements of the 7th Infantry Division and long-range capabilities of the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force. Part of the unit’s mission is to operate in space, cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum and use long-range fires to help the rest of the Joint Force maneuver, including by opening gaps in China’s anti-access/area-denial network — the air, sea and land-based sensors and weapons designed to keep U.S. forces at bay.
“For us in the Pacific, we really are looking at a specific pacing threat and an anti-access/area-denial network,” against which MDC-P aims to create “windows of opportunity for that Joint Force, whether it be a carrier strike group that’s going to pulse into the weapons engagement zone , whether it be a bomber task force, whether it be a ground unit doing a joint forcible-entry operation,” Harrington said.
High-altitude balloons, or HABs, could facilitate that by carrying “launched effects” — the Army’s term for an aerial system deployed from crewed and uncrewed vehicles for reconnaissance, communications, strikes and other missions. HABs would give MDC-P soldiers more ways to employ attack drones and munitions that are cheaper than “exquisite” missiles, available in greater numbers and harder for adversaries to spot.
Interest in HABs has grown in part due to technological improvements that allow them to stay aloft for weeks or months at a time and give operators more control over where they go. That enhances balloons’ value as platforms for radars and other sensors which, at operating altitudes above 60,000 feet, can see far into rival territory while remaining in international airspace. They also offer a cost-effective complement to satellites, which are more expensive and whose orbits limit their time over any one area.
Harrington described high-altitude balloons as part of “an ecosystem” of data-collecting assets in space, in the air, on land and at sea. HABs in particular could compensate if space-based assets are taken out , Harrington said. “So our ability to employ HABs [and] have HABs be persistent enables both our collection and targeting as well as us [to] provide that information to the Joint Force for their collection and targeting.”
Harrington also described a role for balloon- or unmanned surface vessel-launched effects in kinetic strikes. With the right timing and enough precision, those strikes may not even need to eliminate their target to create an opening.
“Maybe I don’t necessarily need to sink a ship, but if I take out certain systems on that vessel, well, then it creates this temporal window of opportunity,” Harrington said.
“We saw great value [in] that maybe I don’t have to use specifically or unmask an exquisite system to achieve that effect. If I can achieve effect of mass utilizing lower-cost systems, maybe that will get me there,” Harrington added. “So we modeled that, and what we saw was — particularly with our unmanned surface vessels, long-range one-way attack, long-range launched effects — the ability to synchronize and mass that could potentially get us to achieve that effect.”
Harrington’s command experimented with some of those systems during Bayonet Quest 26, an exercise held in Michigan and on Lake Huron from late September to early October. An official video showed soldiers working with air and maritime drones, including a quadcopter launched from a surface vessel and a fixed-wing drone hooked up to a balloon. Harrington said Bayonet Quest tested MDC-P’s ability to “orchestrate those systems” by launching them, gathering data from their sensors, and using AI and LLMs to process that data and produce tasking orders.
“If you see [a potential target], then task a UAS to be able to come over and actually validate if that meets the target folder,” Harrington said, describing the approach. “Then I can task long-range one-way attack [or] an attack USV to be able to achieve that effect or I could send that as a potential fire mission to a more exquisite munition to be able to close that kill chain.”
That reduces the need for a large, easily targetable ground presence, Harrington added: “This is all about integration: Integrate multiple systems into one data layer, be able to lay something like a large language model on top of it, and allow orchestration so we don’t have a lot of soldiers in fixed sites on ground control stations.”
Harrington’s comments come amid a flurry of HAB-related experiments by the Army in North Africa , the Middle East , Europe and the Pacific.
At exercise Valiant Shield in Guam this summer, soldiers experimented with HABs and launched effects “within an island-chain operational construct.” One test sent a HAB aloft towing a long-endurance drone “to evaluate stratospheric payload deployment capabilities.” Soldiers tested the same balloon-drone combo in Japan during Orient Shield in September.
The Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Europe has done dozens of HAB launches over the past year to examine the logistics of employing balloons and to test sensing and communications capabilities using “ experimental payloads .”
Speaking alongside Harrington this month, MDC-E commander Brig. Gen. Steven Carpenter said HABs have a role, alongside other sensors and weapons, in opening “windows of opportunity” against anti-access/area-denial networks, in particular by providing resilient communications and additional strike platforms.
“We like to proliferate the stratosphere with high-altitude balloons, but I mean 200, 300 at a time. We like to use them as drones, [communications retransmission], electromagnetic sensing, electronic attack, and then to drop them down and have air-launched effects,” Carpenter said. “During different seasons, the flight paths are different. We study that. We understand during what seasons, where the best places are to launch those high-altitude systems and then, again, to hold enemy cities and capabilities at risk at any time.”

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling cites money-laundering case
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva .
The ruling was issued by Alexandre de Moraes, the same supreme court justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.
The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme . The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.
In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special immunity afforded to officeholders.
He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.
Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.
Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title_orig: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
articles.title_zh: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
articles.content_orig:
Turns out, OpenAI might be really good at computers.
On Monday, the company said it punctured the Exponential Time Hypothesis, or ETH, the nearly 30-year-old belief in the computer science community that some logic problems get overwhelmingly time-consuming as they grow. Hours later, Anthropic released its own research refuting ETH.
OpenAI said it had asked a group of outside computer scientists to organize an open review of its claim. The researchers have highlighted that their involvement is not an endorsement.
If the AI labs' announcements hold, they would likely reopen the hunt for increasingly capable algorithms — something that computer scientists had largely assumed couldn't get much better.
The ultra-nerdy claim has been a huge topic of conversation across social media and in techie circles. Here's how some of the thought leaders have reacted to OpenAI's announcement:
Williams, one of the three independent algorithm design experts who are researching OpenAI's claims, has not certified the company's results.
He wrote on X that, if OpenAI's claim turns out to be true, the fresh findings "should make every computer scientist put at least a little more weight on the possibility of P = NP," making the company closer to another potential $1 million Millennium Prize Problem .
In more practical terms, Williams said the claimed breakthrough could lead to "faster algorithms."
He has previously said that he doesn't believe in ETH.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Marcus, a frequent AI skeptic , wrote that this could be "a big deal if correct," on X.
In a blog post , Cook said OpenAI's claims — while impressive — didn't finally answer computer science's biggest open question.
"The status of P = NP is still unknown," he wrote. "While 3-SAT does not take exponential time, it still takes more than polynomial time as far as anyone knows."
Rivera wrote on X that OpenAI's fresh claim was a reminder that humans could have underestimated a computer's intelligence.
"The bitter lesson should make this unsurprising," he wrote. "I know this logically, but... wow, we really don't know anything."
Gowers wrote a blunt take on X about the development: "Very surprising and consequential that it is false."
Shipper, the AI-pilled chief executive at a tech startup, wrote on X what everyone else was thinking…
"I regret not getting a Ph.D. in frontier math," he said. "(Not that I ever considered getting one but still)."

The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday .
It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments.
The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.
This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles . Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups.
According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.

articles.title_orig: The Super Mouse puts a touchscreen macro pad under your hand
articles.title_zh: The Super Mouse puts a touchscreen macro pad under your hand
articles.content_orig:
Arctic Fox Technologies has announced Super Mouse , a productivity-focused, screen-equipped mouse with built-in, customizable app shortcuts.
As Arctic Fox explains, the computer mouse has employed a relatively consistent form and function for many decades. Peripherals have gotten better and more precise, of course, but the core functionality has remained static. The company hopes to change that with Super Mouse.
Super Mouse is part mouse and part software hub. It integrates software shortcuts, macros, application controls, and other common computer actions directly into the hardware while still serving as a traditional mouse.
“The way people work has completely changed, but the mouse has stayed almost the same for decades,” says Arctic Fox Technologies’ founder and CEO, Sridhar Thirunakara. “We wanted to create a device that keeps the simplicity and comfort people already know while giving them direct access to the tools they use every day.”
The Super Mouse has a built-in 3.1-inch 720 x 720-pixel touchscreen that lets users access a control panel, digital keyboard, and on-screen sliders, such as for photo editing. It includes things like a quick-glance Google Calendar and app shortcuts.
It also includes two customizable physical keys, called Hyper Keys, near the scroll wheel. The mouse also includes a built-in microphone for voice-to-text AI functionality and a gyro for additional control options.
The Super Mouse works alongside a dedicated app, Flow, where users can configure their shortcuts, app integrations, display layouts, and more. There’s no limit to how many apps can have configured shortcuts.
Super Mouse is a wired mouse that connects via USB-C. It works on both macOS and Windows.
The new device is launching first on Kickstarter , with early-bird pricing starting at $199, a 50% discount compared to the expected MSRP. The Super Mouse comes in yellow, white, and dark gray. Arctic Fox says the first units will ship to backers in February 2027 and notes it has been testing prototypes for over a year. However, as always, Kickstarter backers incur risk.

articles.title_orig: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.title_zh: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.content_orig:
Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.
The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.
Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.
TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.
Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.
China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.
While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.
Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

articles.title_orig: Law firm Weil prepares for possible wind-down as crisis deepens
articles.title_zh: Law firm Weil prepares for possible wind-down as crisis deepens
articles.content_orig:
The partner set to take over leadership of Weil, Gotshal & Manges has held talks to leave the firm for a rival, a move that would compound ongoing talent drain at one of Wall Streetâs top dealmaking and restructuring shops.
Ramona Nee, Weilâs co-managing partner, has had discussions to join Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee, an adviser to big private equity firms including Advent, was slated to take over as Weilâs sole chair in January.
Weil declined to comment. Nee did not return a request for comment. Her departure is not guaranteed and the talks could fall apart, the people said.
If she does leave, she would follow a flood of Weilâs top talent out the door and the breakdown of merger talks with crosstown rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Rainmaker Michael Aiello defected to Cravath, Swaine & Moore with a team of partners. It would be likely that a sizable portion of Weilâs Boston partnership would leave with her, according to one person familiar with the matter who is close with many of Weilâs top Boston lawyers.
Nee had told Weil partners she would not take the chair job, which was announced last spring, according to a person briefed on the communication. The Financial Times earlier reported that decision.
Remaining and former Weil lawyers place blame on Aielloâs departure â and Neeâs possible departure â at the feet of executive partner Barry Wolf, who has helmed the firm to some success for more than a decade but in recent years has failed to convince senior partners that Weil has a vision for a world where AI and outsize pay packages upend the perceived usefulness of high-end legal advice.
Aielloâs departure came as a result, in part, because top Weil leaders including Wolf failed to lay out a convincing long-term vision for the firm, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump Jr. Hunted In Mongolia With Russian Oligarch Umar Kremlev Who Bankrolled His Wedding, Report Says
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump Jr. Hunted In Mongolia With Russian Oligarch Umar Kremlev Who Bankrolled His Wedding, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump apepars at a rally at Alico Arena on the Florida Gulf Coast University campus on Oct. 23, 2026, in Fort Myers, Florida.
A woman who had accused President Donald Trump of sexually assaulting her in 1993 described it to congressional staff as rape and said the interaction left her bleeding and bruised, according to a report released Monday by Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee examining Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
Beatrice Keul, a model and former Miss Switzerland, alleged to Judiciary Committee staff that she was raped by Trump in a Plaza Hotel suite in Manhattan when she was 24. Keul said that while attending the American Dream Pageant, which had a partnership with Trump, she met with Trump at a press luncheon at the event.
Trump, according to Keul, promised to arrange her visa in the U.S. and ensure her acceptance into New York University through his friend Paolo Zampolli, a close Trump ally who was, until earlier this month, part of his Administration. At the same event, she also spent at least 10 minutes talking to Epstein who she said claimed to have organized “many parties with Don.”
Later that day, Keul alleges, Trump invited her to a hotel suite where Trump “grabbed Keul from behind and forcibly raped her,” causing “bleeding and bruising on multiple parts of her body,” the report says. Following the incident, Keul alleges Trump made her promise she would keep quiet and repeated his promise for visa and college admission.
Because Keul’s passport had been taken from her on her arrival, she was not able to leave the contest following the incident, she alleges, according to the report. After she returned to Switzerland, she declined to participate in an additional Trump-sponsored pageant in Hawaii several weeks later.
TIME has been unable to independently verify details of Keul’s account.
In a statement, the White House denies the allegations and says that President Trump has been “fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.” “This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis says.
Keul has previously spoken in public about her sexual assault allegations against Trump, but the report provided new details of the alleged rape—as well as reviewing similar accounts of other Trump accusers.
Read more: Trump Said He Banned Epstein From Mar-a-Lago. A Lawmaker Who Reviewed Unredacted Files Says They Tell a Different Story
In addition to Keul’s account, the report also compiled allegations from four other women who have directly accused Trump of rape or sexual assault in connection with the Epstein investigation. The allegations, spanning from the mid-1980s to the 1990s, had all been previously made public either through media interviews or FBI testimony released as part of the Epstein files.
The report’s release, just over a week before Election Day, comes as Democrats are working to signal to voters how they will make use of their power if they gain control of one or both chambers of Congress.
On Monday, Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat of the House Judiciary Committee, called on the Department of Justice to appoint an independent special counsel to oversee the investigation of allegations mentioned in the report. So far, Ghislaine Maxwell , a longtime Epstein confidant, is the only person to have been convicted of sex trafficking of minors in connection with the Epstein case.
“An independent special counsel must investigate Epstein’s co-conspirators and DOJ’s cover-up and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have the evidence they need to pursue justice,” Raskin said in a statement.
The report also alleges that Zampolli, a former Trump administration official and a close Trump ally, was “an active participant” in the Epstein sex trafficking allegations.
According to the report, which cites multiple FBI reports included in the Epstein files, Zampolli arranged U.S. visas for young female models before they met Epstein. One FBI report mentioned that Zampolli arranged an 18-year-old model’s visa before she was recruited to give a massage at Epstein’s house, where Epstein allegedly raped her.
Zampolli himself has also been accused of rape and sexual assault in a separate case brought by model Victoria Drake, who alleges in an ongoing civil lawsuit that Zampolli drugged and raped her in 2023.
TIME has reached out to Zampolli for comment.
Previously, Zampolli has claimed that he had introduced First Lady Melania Trump to the President in 1998, but the report disputes that claim, citing two accounts—one from an unnamed Epstein associate and the other from Amanda Ungaro, a Brazilian model—saying that Epstein had introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump.
The New York Times reported in March that Zampolli had asked a top official at Immigration and Customs Enforcement  last year to detain and deport Ungaro, whom Zampolli had previously dated, amid a custody battle over their son. Zampolli denied making such requests.
Until earlier this month, Zampolli held a diplomatic role under the State Department as Special Representative for Global Partnerships. He was fired two weeks ago over a months-long dispute with the department’s deputy secretary, according to Politico .

articles.title_orig: Everything Apple Announced This Week So Far: New iPad And MacBooks
articles.title_zh: Everything Apple Announced This Week So Far: New iPad And MacBooks
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of its 'Pro and Tell' event, the company has already launched a few new devices.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. It's expected that Apple will unveil a touchscreen MacBook as well.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
We'll update this story if and when Apple makes more announcements. In the meantime, here's everything Apple has announced so far this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders open on October 28, and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders open October 28 and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.
