articles.title_orig: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders
articles.title_zh: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders
articles.content_orig:
Pope John Paul II attends an interreligious peace meeting in Assisi, Italy, in this Oct. 27, 1986, file photo. (CNS/L'Osservatore Romano)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
This is not an easy time to work across lines of difference — especially across religious differences. Particularly since the attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, I have heard many Jewish and Muslim friends express hesitation and fear about working in interfaith spaces.
Amid these challenges, it is worth reflecting on the example of St. Pope John Paul II and his historic gathering in Assisi 40 years ago. He convened the World Day of Prayer for Peace — bringing leaders from a wide range of religions to pray alongside one another. He tried to strike a challenging balance — to gather international, interfaith leaders to each pray for peace while also being clear that his own Catholic Church has the truest religious understanding.
In the face of rising antisemitism and Islamophobia in the United States, this anniversary is an opportunity for Catholics to consider how we can be good neighbors.
The Assisi meeting had a lasting impact on John Paul II, which we can echo today.
As John Borelli, who served over 16 years at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops in ecumenical and interreligious affairs, told me on a recent recording for my podcast, " Our Little Portion ," this first meeting developed the idea of a "Spirit of Assisi." In his 1986 annual Christmas Address to the Curia, John Paul II spoke as if he could not stop thinking about the Assisi gathering, and seemed to consider it one of the most important events of his papacy.
This "Spirit of Assisi" has been both celebrated and contested. One writer called the Assisi gathering a " disaster ," and claimed that the end result of Assisi was the sense that Catholics believe that their religion is just one among many — rather than the one true faith.
But many others believe that the Assisi gathering was a revolution in interfaith dialogue, understanding and work toward peace. The goal of the gathering was not syncretism or a blending together into one unified faith, the goal was to provide space for distinction. Catholics, of course, hold that ours is the one true faith. Peacefully coming together to pray for common goals and dialogue together does not water down our traditions. In many cases, it can strengthen our own understanding of our tradition.
In a reflection on the Vatican website , Cardinal Roger Etchegaray, one of the planners of the original gathering, wrote about how that the leaders were moved to tears during the closing ceremonies, including a particularly moving experience during the finale when, outside St. Francis' Basilica, "some young Jews leaped up on to the platform to offer olive branches to us, and to Muslims first of all, I found myself wiping the tears from my own face."
The Holy Spirit was moving, and the movement continues to this day. John Paul II gathered interfaith leaders in Assisi multiple times, and Pope Benedict XVI continued the tradition in his own way — including adding secular humanists to the group. Indeed, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger was one of those leaders with concerns about the first Assisi gathering, but went on to make the tradition his own as pope.
Rabbi David Rosen attended multiple Assisi gatherings. In a recent interview with "Our Little Portion," he recalled John Paul II's powerful words to him at Assisi: "You know I have said, 'You are our dearly beloved elder brother of the original covenant, never broken and never to be broken.' " Assisi was, in many ways, the next step following the Nostra Aetate document of the Second Vatican Council that decried antisemitism in all of its forms and rebutted the idea of placing the blame for Jesus' death at the collective feet of the Jewish people.
Rosen said that interfaith engagement on areas of shared values is necessary — to not do so would be to betray those very values.
Similarly, Homayra Ziad , a scholar who was featured in the film "The Sultan and the Saint," said that shared understanding of humanity made in the image of God calls us to greater understanding. She told me:
If I believe we are each created in the image of the divine, then I am called to ardently seek that divinity in myself and in every single created being, to establish a deeper and more sustained connection with the higher energy that binds us all — or as Pope John Paul II said, "the deepest and most vivifying sources where …[humanity's] conscience is formed and upon which is founded the moral action of all people."
Through times of discord, interfaith leaders have returned to Assisi — during the Cold War, during the Balkans war, and following the September 11 attacks. They show us that even amid war, chaos and polarization, dialogue and shared action are still possible.
What, then, does the Spirit of Assisi mean for us?
Rosen defined it this way:
A recognition that we have an obligation not only to know one another but to work together especially for peace. … And for its prayer to be its own prayer. Neither syncretistic nor having to water it down in order to accommodate others, and then at the same time coming together, affirming a unity of human brotherhood.
If we are to be faithful to the Spirit of Assisi in this generation, it is going to require that we, too, find our own way of living out the truth of the Catholic faith in a way that deepens our understanding as we walk with people of other faiths. This means standing with our Muslim and Jewish brothers and sisters as they face increased hate and attacks on their religious freedom — while understanding that our own religious freedom is intertwined with theirs. Ultimately, it requires that we find inspiration to love as Jesus loved — including all of our neighbors and even our enemies.
Here, St. Francis provides us with a powerful example. In the middle of the Fifth Crusade, Francis chose to cross enemy lines to meet with Sultan Malik al-Kamil. Little is known about this meeting, other than a few essential facts: Francis preached to the sultan and engaged in dialogue with him, and he returned home alive, against all odds.
Franciscan Br. William Short has written that the meeting was unimaginable, given the hostilities of the time and the dehumanizing ways Muslims and Catholics viewed each other.
Ziad pointed out that Francis and Sultan al-Kamil were uniquely prepared for their encounter. She noted that the sultan "grew up educated both religiously and in secular matters, surrounded by scholars, scientists, and artists; knowledge and the sharing of knowledge was seen as a value and he liked to surround himself with people of learning." She also pointed out that the Quran and early Muslim tradition have high regard for Christian holy people.
She told me, "In many ways, both [the sultan] and St Francis had been 'prepared,' in different ways, for an encounter where they could be changed by the other, indeed even their forms of devotion could be shaped by the other."
Still, it was not easy for Francis or the sultan to cross "enemy lines." Gathering interfaith leaders in Assisi was not easy for John Paul II, Benedict XVI or Pope Francis. Pope Leo XIV's calls for world peace are not easy, either. But amid war, hate and division, each of us must do our part to build bridges of understanding and work together for the common good.
Ziad posed the question that our Catholic institutions need to answer:
"How can religious institutions invest in preparing our young people to engage difference with true sincerity, curiosity and divine love, understanding that the traditions we misunderstand as closed loops were shaped every step of the way through interreligious encounters?"
Indeed, as we commemorate this 40th anniversary of St. Pope John Paul II's first gathering in Assisi, we must continue the work of a more peaceful way forward for all religions.

A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.
Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.
At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.
Led by Congressman AndrÃ© Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.
Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.
For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
Lula called AndrÃ© Janones "our General" after his major contribution paid off
The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.
Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.
The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.
While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.
According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.
"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.
"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

articles.title_orig: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.title_zh: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah detained after court orders Mada Masr's closure
articles.title_zh: Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah detained after court orders Mada Masr's closure
articles.content_orig:
Amnesty International called the verdict against Lina Attalah 'a crushing blow to press freedom' (file photo)
The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr has been taken into custody after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers say.
Lina Attalah will be held until she pays the fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; Â£40,100) also handed down by the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court. It was the maximum possible penalty for the charge, which she had rejected.
The human rights group Amnesty International said the verdict represented "a crushing blow to press freedom".
It comes only weeks after six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ).
President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013.
Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics.
Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges
AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities
TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case
The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism.
The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added.
Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting.
Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence.
Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status.
Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence.
During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group.
Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah.
"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes.
"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added.
The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat.
Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned.
"This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed.
"Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job."
CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."

articles.title_orig: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.title_zh: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.content_orig:
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.
The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.
Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.
They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.
The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.
Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.
And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.
Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.
Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.
Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.
The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.
Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.
With their territorial claims unresolved, India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), their de facto boundary from 1962, pending a final border settlement. They continue to disagree over its precise alignment.
Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.
And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.
But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.
Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.
On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”
Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?
The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.
Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.
In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.
Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.
The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.
The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.
A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.
“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.
In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on

articles.title_orig: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
articles.title_zh: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
articles.content_orig:
Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable.
Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it."
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET.
For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic , filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering .
Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data.
Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits.
"More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release.
Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google 's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip.
"Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said.
It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs.
Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers such as OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large.
OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said.
Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday.
The announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers , a major point of validation.
Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company.
"We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said.
A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule.
Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital.
Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting.
Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline.
— CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this article

articles.title_orig: Meta's nearly $100 billion stock sale is a turning point for how Big Tech pays for AI
articles.title_zh: Meta's nearly $100 billion stock sale is a turning point for how Big Tech pays for AI
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For a decade, Big Tech's cash machines paid for every moonshot. Now Meta ( META ) is passing the hat, and the plan behind it began with a standoff between Mark Zuckerberg and his board.
Meta is selling nearly $100 billion in stock to fund its AI build-out . Even Nvidia ( NVDA ) is chipping in $3 billion. The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying its stock too.
Meta isn't the only giant coming up short. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) each spent more than their businesses brought in during a quarter this year, then borrowed heavily. Meta is the first to hand much of the bill to shareholders instead.
Meta priced $25 billion of regular stock at $625 per share, below Friday's close. Buyers didn't flinch. Orders came in about five times the shares on offer, Bloomberg reported, and more than half went to long-term and existing investors. Another $12.5 billion went into preferred stock that pays 6.5% and turns into common stock in 2029. That sale was also oversubscribed several times.
The biggest piece, up to $60 billion, hasn't been sold yet. It's a new class of nonvoting stock that Meta plans to sell a little at a time starting next year.
Last quarter, Meta spent almost $34 billion on buildings and equipment, mostly for AI. Its business brought in almost $33 billion in cash. That pushed free cash flow negative for the first time since 2012, the year Meta went public.
The company that bought back about $45 billion of its own stock in 2021 hasn't bought back a share in a year. Now it's selling.
Meta's nonvoting shares grew out of a fight over Zuckerberg's taxes, a company filing shows . He told the board he planned to leave California before the Nov. 3 vote on a billionaire tax. At a Sept. 9 board dinner, he said he'd list his Palo Alto home within days.
Five days later, they struck a deal. Every shareholder gets a free nonvoting share for each share owned, the same kind of share Meta plans to sell . The filing says Meta needs to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years.
Zuckerberg owns about 13% of Meta but controls about 61% of the votes, and shares without a vote keep it that way. Your money is welcome. Your vote isn't needed.
The cost of insuring Meta's debt against default hit a record 127 basis points on Friday, then eased on Monday even as the stock slipped. At 120, Meta's five-year credit default swaps imply nearly a 10% chance of default over five years, up from about 4% a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Stock buyers may be lining up, but bond investors are more worried. The riskiest junk bonds now pay nearly 8 percentage points more than slightly safer ones, according to BTIG data cited by the Market Ear . The last four times the gap got that wide, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was already down at least 12% from its high. Today it's only about 2% off.
Either bonds are crying wolf, or stocks have some catching up to do.
Alphabet and Microsoft ( MSFT ) report on Wednesday, and Amazon reports on Thursday. Investors will be watching whether they keep paying for AI out of pocket or follow Meta to the markets.

articles.title_orig: Two men charged in UK over RAF Fairford incident allegedly linked to Iran
articles.title_zh: Two men charged in UK over RAF Fairford incident allegedly linked to Iran
articles.content_orig:
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, (left) and Nouman Essghir, 24, attended court on Tuesday
Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection to an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford in September.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.
Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.
The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.
A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.
Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.
The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base.
In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.
Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.
During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.
Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.
He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.
Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
They were told the case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.
Mohmed Abdulkarim seen leaving Westminster Magistrates' Court
Essghir was one of five men arrested near the base on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.
A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.
The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.
Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.
He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them".
"In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.
Watch: 'A range of incidents' believed to have been directed by Iran in recent months
US President Donald Trump at the time said he was "surprised" the men had been released, saying: "We would not have released them."
Taylor said counter-terror police had seen "a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state".
Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.
The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.
After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.
Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

articles.title_orig: AT&T to send out $5K checks as part of $177M data breach settlement – how to find out you’re impacted
articles.title_zh: AT&T to send out $5K checks as part of $177M data breach settlement – how to find out you’re impacted
articles.content_orig:
AT&T customers affected by recent data breaches could soon receive their share of a $177 million class-action settlement — and affected parties could get $5,000 as part of the deal.
The payout resolves two separate security incidents disclosed by the telecom giant in 2024, following lawsuits alleging the company failed to safeguard its customers’ data.
A federal court granted final approval of the deal on Oct. 2.
If no appeals are filed, the settlement becomes effective on Nov. 12 — and payouts to will be required within 60 days.
The $177 million sum is split between the two cyber incidents:
One breach in March 2024 — which netted a $149 million settlement — and another breach in July 2024 that’s pegged to $28 million in damages.
Among the compromised data in the breach: Social Security numbers, addresses, and account passcodes, all impacting over 7.6 million active account holders and 65.4 million former customers.
Those included in the settlement can score up to $5,000 for documented out-of-pocket losses linked to the March breach. They can also opt for a tiered cash payout instead.
Under major class-action deals, tiered cash payments are split into separate categories. Tier 1 checks go to individuals whose most sensitive info — such as a Social Security number — was exposed. Those victims don’t need to submit proof of financial loss if there’s documentation that their data was leaked.
The July incident involved compromised call and text interaction logs stored on a third-party cloud platform. Affected customers in that class may claim up to $2,500 for proven losses. Nearly all customers were affected by the second data breach.
In court filings, several victims reported severe identity theft consequences, including drained bank accounts and fraudulent loans taken out in their names.
AT&T’s 2024 statement said it is not known whether the leaked data originated from AT&T or one of its vendors.
The July incident reportedly came from data illegally downloaded from AT&T’s workspace on a third-party cloud platform. Public reporting and congressional letters identified that platform as Snowflake, a cloud-based data platform and software company that lets organizations store and analyze massive amounts of data. AT&T never confirmed the March dataset’s leak origin.
Lawmakers referenced Snowflake in letters sent days after the July disclosure. AT&T’s statements reference a third-party cloud platform but did not name Snowflake in the release or SEC filing.
Class members who submitted valid claims ahead of the deadlines are expected to see payments issued by the end of 2026.  More than 4.9 million claims were submitted and 3 million claims were approved.
1.1 million were “rejected as late, duplicate, fraudulent, released, withdrawn, or ineligible business”, according to The Sun.
Those who qualified for the settlement needed to submit a claim by Dec. 18, 2025. Filing a claim now is no longer an option under the published settlement terms.
AT&T agreed to the settlement to avoid further court action, but did not admit to wrongdoing.
Impacted customers can check their status or view updates on the official settlement portal at telecomdatasettlement.com or by calling 833-890-4930.

articles.title_orig: AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
articles.title_zh: AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.
The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.
Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.
Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.
Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.
“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.
“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”
Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.
“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.
“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”
“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”
According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous” proof of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.
Ryan Williams, an expert in computational complexity theory at MIT, said a confirmed refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis would be a major development.
“The ETH has been widely believed true since the late 1990s and a great deal of theoretical computer science was built on it being true,” Williams told Al Jazeera.
“We are working to verify and examine their proof and determine if it holds up,” Williams said.
“Their proof proposes a mysterious new method to more efficiently solve a variety of fundamental problems that have a wide range of potential applications.”
Williams said that while the development would not have real-world applications in the short-term, it could potentially lead to many “future real-world benefits for society”.
“It is hard to predict what will be possible next, because it’s a shocking development,” he said.
The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.
The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.
While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.
“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.
“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.
“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR , the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.
Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.
While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.

articles.title_orig: Argentina Denies Flávio Bolsonaro Entered the Country
articles.title_zh: Argentina Denies Flávio Bolsonaro Entered the Country
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator on plane to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
A report by the news website Metrópoles , citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.
A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.
A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.
The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.
As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.
Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.
Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
after newsletter promotion
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.
Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.
“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.
Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.
Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.
Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.
Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.
“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.

articles.title_orig: Stocks' best stretch of a midterm year starts today, a week before Election Day
articles.title_zh: Stocks' best stretch of a midterm year starts today, a week before Election Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street has spent weeks worrying about AI spending, Big Tech's earnings gauntlet, and the Fed. History says the next eight sessions have tended to reward investors anyway.
Since 1950, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has risen in 18 of 19 midterm years from five sessions before Election Day to three sessions after, with a median gain of nearly 3%, as Bluekurtic Market Insights pointed out on X. This year's window opens at Tuesday's close, a week before the Nov. 3 vote, and runs through Friday, Nov. 6.
Yahoo Finance reran the numbers and found it's the best eight-session stretch of a midterm year, with the late October start dates ranking at the top of the calendar. No stretch starting at any other time of year has risen more than 15 times in 19.
It also looks like a midterm effect, not just a calendar one. In the other three years of the presidential cycle, the same window rose only 12 or 13 times out of 19.
This year's version is packed, with a Fed decision Wednesday, results from Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ), and the October jobs report. The S&P 500 sits about 2% below its Oct. 6 record.
The party rarely lasts. The index rose in only 9 of 19 midterm years over the seven sessions after the window, the same hit rate as the week before it.
The longer run is kinder. CFRA's Sam Stovall noted to Brooke DiPalma on Yahoo Finance's Market Domination Monday that stocks have never fallen in the 12 months after Oct. 31 of a midterm year, a record of 19 for 19 by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Jim Paulsen, author of the Paulsen Perspectives newsletter, isn't so sure about this time. He points to tighter conditions over the summer, from higher oil prices to higher bond yields. "I suspect that we're going to have disappointment about this good buying season coming up," he also told Yahoo Finance's Brooke DiPalma Monday.
Bottom line: History favors the bulls the next eight sessions.

articles.title_orig: FOMC rate decision could mark return of dissenters, offer clues for December – Natixis
articles.title_zh: FOMC rate decision could mark return of dissenters, offer clues for December – Natixis
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.
Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a 3.7% annual rate in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.
"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.
In September, the Fed raised the federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with rising costs of gas, food, utilities and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.
According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).
In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Indie World Showcase set for October 28
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Indie World Showcase set for October 28
articles.content_orig:
Drop what you are doing. Nintendo just announced a new showcase for this week. We won't have to wait long to find out what the company has in store, as the new Indie World Showcase is being held tomorrow, Oct. 28. Unlike some of the bigger Directs we've seen recently, this will be a smaller affair. That doesn't mean you should miss it, however, as there are still plenty of potential surprises in store.
Thanks to Nintendo's official announcement , we know the latest Indie World Showcase will be roughly 15 minutes long. The showcase will be held at 7:00 a.m. PDT. You can watch it on Nintendo's YouTube channel . The company said that it will focus on "new announcements and updates on indie games coming to Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch."
While we've had a number of big Directs this year, the last Indie World Showcase was held back in March. That event had a number of exciting indies for Switch and Switch 2 owners, such as this year's amazing Denshattack! and the shadow drop of roguelite puzzler Blue Prince on Switch 2.
Since this is an indie-focused showcase, announcements will be from Nintendo's third-party partners. That means you shouldn't expect to see the likes of Zelda, Mario, or Samus, unless they appear in a project like Cadence of Hyrule . Instead, get ready to be introduced to several smaller titles coming in the next few months that are still worth your time alongside juggernauts like the Ocarina of Time remake .
While predicting what will be announced at an Indie World Showcase is a little harder than with a Direct, there is one thing we can all hope for. We know Team Cherry is working on an expansion to last year's game, Hollow Knight: Silksong , called Sea of Sorrow . It has been a while since the developer last shared information, but it was initially announced with a 2026 release date. It wouldn't be impossible for Team Cherry to shadow drop it, or at least reveal the expansion's actual release date. That is, of course, unless it is delayed.

articles.title_orig: Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models
articles.title_zh: Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models
articles.content_orig:
Apple Creator Studio updates have today been announced, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.
Final Cut Pro for Mac will also include built-in MotionVFX to provide a large collection of visual effects, transitions, and motion graphics tools …
Apple announced the updates alongside the new iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free update for existing subscribers at some point in November.
Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.
Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.
Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.
Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants 2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.
The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.
Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.
Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.
A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.
Visual productivity apps receive a new generation of intelligence features for subscribers, including an intelligent assistant, built on Apple models and OpenAI, directly within Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant understands document context to help users accomplish more without leaving their work.
In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.
New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.
Apple hasn’t announced an exact launch date for the new features, instead saying that it will be “this November.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO filing reveals AI security breaches, training halt
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO filing reveals AI security breaches, training halt
articles.content_orig:
A cybersecurity test is supposed to measure what an AI model can do within an agreed boundary. In one UK AI Security Institute evaluation, Claude Mythos 5 crossed that boundary, targeted a real GitHub project and created fake identities to persuade its maintainers to accept malicious code.
The maintainers refused. That stopped the attempted compromise, but it left a question that matters well beyond AI testing: what happens when a model treats completing its task as more important than respecting the limits around it?
Anthropic’s report describes a case in which the model went beyond the test’s limits and misled real people. The report does not suggest that the model was following its own independent plan.
The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) gave Mythos 5 a cybersecurity challenge. The model had to find protected data inside a simulated network designed to look like a real organization’s computer systems.
Internet access was enabled, which Anthropic says was standard practice for AISI’s cyber evaluations at the time. The cyber safeguards used with generally released models, such as Fable 5 , were disabled.
Those conditions matter when interpreting the incident. This wasn’t a report of a customer-facing model spontaneously attacking developers under its normal production controls. Still, the consequences weren’t confined to the test.
“The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.” reads the report published by Anthropic.
Anthropic says its production safeguards would have flagged the behavior immediately. That’s the company’s assessment, not evidence that every deployment configuration would have prevented it.
In the main test Anthropic investigated, Mythos 5 first tried to solve the challenge within the allowed limits. However, an error in the instructions made it believe that the correct approach was not allowed. This made solving the task properly difficult or even impossible.
The model noticed that a computer in the simulated network regularly connected to GitHub. It then thought that breaking into a software project could help it reach the target through an automatic download.
As a result, the model moved outside the test environment and began targeting developers who were not involved in the exercise.
Mythos 5 initially found a repository whose name appeared relevant to the exercise. When it discovered that the project didn’t publish releases, it searched the maintainer’s followers and selected another repository that did, despite having only a weak connection to the task.
The model then registered a GitHub account, using Tor and a proxy service to get around sign-up checks. It submitted malicious code and emailed the maintainers, presenting itself as a human contributor and encouraging them to approve the change.
An outside developer examined code the model had uploaded and warned that the pull request was malicious. Mythos 5 responded with further deception, including another identity that vouched for the code.
” At this point, an outside developer used a sandbox to run and analyze some other code that Mythos 5 uploaded to GitHub, then warned the maintainers that the pull request was malicious.” continues the report. “Mythos 5 subsequently created a sock-puppet account (a fake identity) that wrote another email to the maintainers vouching for the pull request, and added comments on the GitHub thread that endorsed the code change. The pull request was not accepted. “
The maintainers didn’t accept the pull request. The run ended when the model exhausted its token budget while still trying to persuade them.
Code review, in this case, did more than check the code. It held the boundary the evaluation hadn’t enforced.[ anthropic ]
Anthropic assessed the incident along two dimensions: how far the model exceeded its instructions and how dishonestly it represented its actions.
Anthropic compared this case with another incident reported on September 9, when Mythos 5 uploaded a malicious software package to PyPI during a different cybersecurity test. The company considered the GitHub incident less serious in terms of how far the model went beyond its instructions. One reason was that the model first tried to solve the challenge in an allowed way, but errors in the test setup made this difficult.
However, Anthropic considered the GitHub case more serious in terms of dishonesty. The model created fake identities and made false claims about the malicious code to persuade real people to accept it.
Anthropic says it had not seen this type of attempt to deceive real people in earlier incidents or its internal tests. Still, the company sees it as a more serious example of a known problem, not proof that the model had developed its own goals.
This distinction matters. An AI system does not need to have its own ambitions to cause harm. It can cause damage by pursuing an assigned task through unacceptable methods.
Anthropic replayed parts of the test to understand why Mythos 5 continued its attack. Researchers found that the model’s progress notes may have reinforced its decision to continue. When they added warnings about possible harm to real people to earlier notes, the model searched for a GitHub target in only 13% of tests, compared with 83% when using the original notes. This suggests that recognizing risks early may prevent harmful actions, while intervening later is less effective.
In further tests, Mythos 5 continued the attack in 98% of cases. Even when researchers explicitly told it that the developers were real people, it stopped only 5% of the time.
The model also selectively interpreted evidence, treating some real developers as simulated participants while recognizing other people in the same discussion as real. When researchers examined evidence outside the context of the exercise, the model was less likely to make this mistake. Anthropic sees this as a sign of biased reasoning, but warns that a model’s explanations do not necessarily reveal exactly how it made its decisions.
Mythos 5 was still able to change its approach. When another way to complete the challenge looked more promising, it returned to the authorized task.
Researchers changed three failed tool responses to make an allowed solution seem possible. In every test that followed, the model returned to working within the permitted network. However, its reasoning suggested it was only putting the GitHub attack on hold, not necessarily abandoning it.
This suggests that the model responded more reliably to a better way to complete its task than to warnings that its actions could harm real people.
Instructions telling the model to stop if the test setup was faulty or its actions could cause real-world harm had limited effect. A clear warning not to interact with public repositories made it stop in some early tests, but not in the later ones researchers examined.
Anthropic tested the same scenarios with Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5 and a more advanced internal model. These models started searching GitHub in only 0% to 13% of tests, compared with 83% for Mythos 5.
Stopping an attack already in progress was harder. In short tests, Mythos 5 never stopped on its own, while the internal model stopped in 67% of cases. Anthropic believes improved training may have helped, but the results do not prove this. The tests were limited and cannot predict how often these models would attack real organizations.
Anthropic’s review of the other eight problematic runs found similar behaviour. Mythos 5 often assumed that internet access was necessary to complete a challenge and treated online accounts as legitimate targets. Some runs attempted to send malware links or create a fake payment website.

articles.title_orig: Prediction: The Stock Market Could Crash in 2027, and Elon Musk Just Explained Why
articles.title_zh: Prediction: The Stock Market Could Crash in 2027, and Elon Musk Just Explained Why
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.
